name: Debra Albert, DNP, RN
title: Chief Nursing Officer & Senior Vice President, Patient Care Services
affiliations: Chief Nursing Officer and Senior Vice President of Patient Care Services at NYU Langone Health since April 2020; she is listed in that role on the 2026 AHA board roster.
AHA Board of Trustees: elected August 2025 to a three-year term that began January 1, 2026 (through 2028).
Former SVP of patient care services and CNO at UChicago Medicine (2012-2020), and CNO roles at Cleveland Clinic's main campus, Fairview Hospital and MacNeal Hospital (Vanguard Health Systems).
Longtime member of American Organization for Nursing Leadership (AONL) committees (2010-2023), the AHA's nursing-leadership affiliate.
NYU Langone named Alec Kimmelman, MD, PhD, previously director of its Perlmutter Cancer Center, in April 2025 to succeed longtime dean and CEO Robert Grossman, MD.
financial: NYU Langone Health reported $15.4 billion in revenue and $482.8 million in operating income in FY2025 (ended Aug. 31, 2025), a 3.1% margin, with $5.7 billion in cash and investments and $1.3 billion in capital spending.

The hospital obligated group alone earned an $809.8 million operating gain on $10.8 billion in revenue in FY2025, a 7.5% margin; the system-wide margin is lower because the medical school lost $329.2 million.
NYU Langone Hospitals' FY2025 Form 990 (EIN 13-3971298) reports $10.49 billion in revenue and $674.8 million in net income, and lists $51.3 million in executive compensation.

Combined across NYU Langone's Form 990s (FY2025), former CEO Robert Grossman was paid $30.29 million: base $5.15M, bonus and incentive $19.68M, other reportable $109,789, retirement and deferred $5.30M, nontaxable benefits $38,385. CFO Joseph Lhota received $14.04 million ($10.32M bonus) and chief clinical officer Andrew Brotman, MD, $10.96 million ($7.0M bonus).
CFO Joseph Lhota was listed at $6.63 million and hospital operations chief Fritz Francois, MD, at $6.43 million in FY2025 reportable compensation.
NYU Langone's FY2024 990 discloses first-class or charter travel and reported conflict-of-interest transactions.

The Lown Institute's 2024 fair-share report (2021 data) ranked NYU Langone Hospitals third worst in the nation with a -$222 million fair-share deficit, meaning its estimated tax breaks exceeded its qualifying community investment by that amount. Lown's 2021 report had put it at -$163 million (sixth worst).
Albert does not appear among the officers and key employees in ProPublica's extracts of the FY2024 and FY2025 hospital filings, so her own pay is not public.
lobbying: Senate LDA filings show NYU Langone spent about $500,000 on federal lobbying in 2025: $210,000 in-house through NYU Langone Hospitals and $290,000 through BGR Government Affairs.
Through the third quarter of 2026, filings show about $390,000 more ($150,000 in-house and $240,000 through BGR), with issues widening to tax, education and immigration.
LDA filings for 2024 total roughly $150,000 ($100,000 in-house after amendments plus $50,000 from BGR, which registered in the fourth quarter).
The AHA itself reported $25.47 million in in-house federal lobbying in 2025 and $14.39 million in the first three quarters of 2026 (Senate LDA filings), the agenda trustees help set.
No notable personal political giving by Albert surfaced.
revolvingDoor: No government roles for Albert were identified.
Her path to the AHA board ran through more than a decade on AONL committees, the AHA's own nursing-leadership pipeline.
homeSystemRecord: NYU Langone Health's charity care at cost was $141M (latest hospital tax returns).
NYU Langone Health has 171 340B contract pharmacy arrangements registered with HRSA (OPAIS registry, Sept. 29, 2026).
FY2025 volumes rose sharply: inpatient discharges up 5%, outpatient surgery up 10.8% and emergency visits up 3.4%, growth the system credits to short lengths of stay and higher patient acuity.
NYU Langone has expanded into affluent outpatient markets on Long Island and in Palm Beach County, Florida, extending the facility-fee footprint the AHA defends against site-neutral payment.

In November 2025 NYU Langone and nine other medical centers sued HHS and Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over a 2023 rule that counts Medicare Part C enrollees in Medicare disproportionate share hospital (DSH) calculations, a rule HHS applied retroactively to payments back to 2004. NYU Langone joined on behalf of its Brooklyn campus.

NYSNA nurses at NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn issued a strike notice in February 2025; the strike was called off. NYU Langone was not among the hospitals in the January-February 2026 New York City nurses strike, which hit NewYork-Presbyterian, Mount Sinai and Montefiore.
In February 2026 NYU Langone announced it would stop providing gender-related medical care to minors, months before settling with the Justice Department.
litigation: On Sept. 18, 2026, NYU Langone settled a Justice Department investigation into its provision of gender-related care to minors. It agreed to permanently end puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and surgery for patients under 18. The DOJ said NYU paid $8.5 million as part of the resolution, while NYU's public notice gives no dollar figure and denies wrongdoing or liability.
NYU Langone is a plaintiff in the November 2025 Medicare DSH suit against HHS; no ruling has been reported.
No 2025-2026 False Claims Act, antitrust, state AG or patient-debt actions against NYU Langone surfaced in searches.
redFlags: NYU Langone posts one of the largest fair-share deficits in the country (-$222 million, third worst in Lown's 2024 report) while sending its nurse executive, not its CEO, to the AHA board.
Its hospitals earned a 7.5% operating margin and $674.8 million in net income in FY2025, yet the system is suing HHS to recover Medicare DSH money tied to low-income patients.

Former CEO Grossman was paid about $20.7 million on the FY2024 filing and at least $17.8 million on the FY2025 filing; total executive pay of $51.3 million and first-class or charter travel sit uneasily with a large fair-share deficit.

In September 2026 NYU Langone settled with the Justice Department, with an $8.5 million payment reported by the DOJ, by permanently ending a category of care for minors, while the deal shielded the patient records the DOJ had demanded.
Outpatient expansion into affluent Long Island and Palm Beach markets builds facility-fee revenue, the exact pricing the AHA lobbies to protect from site-neutral reform.
Federal lobbying spending roughly tripled from about $150,000 in 2024 to about $500,000 in 2025 and is on pace to rise again in 2026 as Medicaid and tax-exemption fights heat up.
patternSummary: NYU Langone is a $15.4 billion academic system whose hospitals earned a 7.5% margin in FY2025. It carries a top-three national fair-share deficit and paid its former CEO about $20.7 million in FY2024, and it is represented on the AHA board by its chief nurse. Albert gives the AHA a clinician face while her employer triples its federal lobbying, sues HHS over DSH dollars and settles with the Justice Department.

name: Robert W. (Rob) Allen
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Intermountain Health since December 2022; he is listed in that role on the 2026 AHA board roster.
AHA Board of Trustees: elected August 2025 to a three-year term that began January 1, 2026 (through 2028).
Former member of the AHA Strategic Leadership Group on Health Systems and the AHA Medicare DSH Advisory Group.
Intermountain COO (2017-2022) and region vice president (2011-2017); earlier ran hospitals in Wyoming, New Jersey and Massachusetts.
Intermountain runs 33 hospitals and more than 385 clinics across seven states and owns SelectHealth, its health plan.
financial: Intermountain reported $18.5 billion in revenue and $515 million in operating income in 2025, a 2.8% operating margin.

Schedule J breakdown (FY2024, Intermountain Health Care Inc. and IHC Health Services): base salary $2.12M, bonus and incentive $3.27M, other reportable $17,786, retirement and deferred $4.18M, nontaxable benefits $122,376; total $9.72M. Bonus and incentive pay was 34% of the total.

The FY2024 Form 990 for IHC Health Services Inc. (EIN 94-2854057), Intermountain's main operating entity, lists Allen at $5,410,130 in reportable compensation plus $4,305,226 in other compensation, about $9.7 million in total.

That is up from about $6.3 million ($3,669,634 plus $2,624,498) on the FY2023 filing, a roughly 54% increase in one year. The filing labels him 'Former Officer' of that entity, so pay from other Intermountain entities may not be included.
IHC Health Services alone reported $10.65 billion in revenue, $1.14 billion in net income and $16.1 billion in net assets in FY2024, up from $844.8 million in net income in FY2023.
The FY2024 990 lists $45.4 million in executive compensation and discloses first-class or charter travel and reported conflict-of-interest transactions.
Former CFO Albert Zimmerli was listed at $8.27 million in reportable compensation on the FY2023 990.
S&P rates Intermountain AA+ (affirmed June 2023), which it describes as the highest rating in U.S. nonprofit health care; no 2025-2026 rating changes surfaced.
lobbying: Intermountain's federal lobbying through McDermott Will & Schulte totaled $230,000 in 2024, $220,000 in 2025 and $150,000 in the first three quarters of 2026, on budget, health care and Medicare/Medicaid issues (Senate LDA filings).
The AHA itself reported $25.47 million in in-house federal lobbying in 2025 and $14.39 million in the first three quarters of 2026 (Senate LDA filings), the agenda trustees help set.
Intermountain maintains a federal PAC, InterMountain Health Care PAC (FEC ID C00166991).
Intermountain relies heavily on the AHA and state hospital associations for federal advocacy, keeping its direct spending low relative to its $18.5 billion size.
revolvingDoor: No government appointments for Allen were identified.
His influence runs through AHA governance: trustee, Health Systems Committee and former Medicare DSH Advisory Group member, plus a featured slot at the 2026 AHA Annual Membership Meeting.
homeSystemRecord: Intermountain Health's charity care at cost was $247.6M (FY2024 hospital tax returns).
Intermountain Health has 427 340B contract pharmacy arrangements registered with HRSA (OPAIS registry, Sept. 29, 2026).

On May 22, 2026, Intermountain announced it would cut 93 caregiver roles effective July 24 'to support long-term financial sustainability,' closing two occupational health clinics and a sports medicine clinic in Colorado and a family medicine clinic in Lewistown, Mont.

In August 2026, 95% of voting members of Montana Nurses Association Local 5, which represents 143 nurses at Intermountain's St. James Hospital in Butte, rejected a proposed contract over retention, recruitment and pay.

In January 2024 Intermountain's Saltzer Health physician group in Idaho, acquired in 2020, announced it would sell or close all its Treasure Valley operations, affecting more than 400 employees and about 80,000 patients a year.
The April 2022 merger with SCL Health created a 33-hospital system spanning Utah, Colorado, Montana, Kansas and beyond; the Colorado AG reviewed and allowed it.
Intermountain owns both hospitals and SelectHealth, a vertical structure that raises steering and network-adequacy concerns in Utah.
Intermountain participates in the 340B program and touts a 340B-funded insulin voucher program, but does not disclose how much 340B margin reaches patients.
No Lown Institute fair-share figure for Intermountain surfaced.
litigation: Utah County v. Intermountain Health Care (Utah Supreme Court, 1985) stripped property-tax exemptions from two Intermountain hospitals and remains a landmark ruling against nonprofit hospital tax exemption.
In April 2013 Intermountain paid $25.5 million to settle False Claims Act allegations tied to Stark Law violations in its physician financial arrangements.
No 2025-2026 False Claims Act, antitrust, state AG or patient-debt actions against Intermountain surfaced in news and legal-database searches.
redFlags: Allen's pay on the main operating entity's 990 jumped about 54% in one year, to roughly $9.7 million in FY2024, shortly before Intermountain began cutting jobs and closing clinics in 2026.

Months after its main entity posted $1.14 billion in FY2024 net income, Intermountain cut 93 jobs and closed rural and specialty clinics in Colorado and Montana in 2026, citing 'financial sustainability.'
Intermountain earned $515 million on operations in 2025 while keeping nonprofit tax exemptions, and its 990 discloses first-class or charter travel and conflict-of-interest transactions.
Vertical integration with SelectHealth gives Intermountain control of both price and coverage across much of Utah.
The 1985 Utah Supreme Court ruling and the 2013 $25.5 million Stark settlement show that Intermountain's tax-exempt status and physician deals have both been successfully challenged before.
As an AHA trustee and former DSH advisory group member, Allen helps steer national positions on DSH, 340B and site-neutral payment that pay off for his own system.
patternSummary: Allen is a career Intermountain operator whose own pay jumped to about $9.7 million in FY2024 while he ran an $18.5 billion, vertically integrated nonprofit that earned $515 million on operations in 2025. In 2026 the system cut jobs and closed clinics in Colorado and Montana despite those profits. Intermountain spends modestly on its own lobbying and leans on the AHA, where Allen now sits as a trustee, to defend 340B, DSH and tax-exemption protections.

name: Michele Baker Richardson, JD
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of HEA Consultants, LLC, a consulting and executive coaching firm.
Immediate past chair of the Advocate Health board; elected vice chair in December 2022 after the Advocate Aurora Health-Atrium Health merger and chair in January 2024.
Previously listed as chair-elect (FY2018-FY2021) and chair (FY2022-FY2023) on Advocate Aurora Health's Form 990 filings.
NACD Directorship Certified.
Affiliated with Ronald McDonald House Atlanta, The Links, Incorporated, Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc., and The Black Directors Health Equity Agenda.
JD from Yale Law School; bachelor's degree in economics and organizational behavior from Brown University.
financial: Advocate Health reported 2025 revenue of more than $38.9 billion, operating income of more than $1.5 billion (a 4.0% margin, up from 3.5%) and a $4.6 billion bottom line driven by about $3 billion in net investment income, with 283 days cash on hand.
Advocate Health's FY2024 Form 990 reports $135,767 paid to Baker Richardson as board chair through related organizations, up from $131,433 in FY2023 as chair-elect.
Advocate Aurora Health's Form 990s report her board pay at $90,966 (FY2018), $132,165 (FY2019), $126,333 (FY2020 and FY2021), $143,767 (FY2022) and $131,433 (FY2023).

On the FY2024 Advocate Health Form 990 filed during her chairmanship, CEO Eugene Woods was reported at $22,870,197 in compensation from related organizations plus $2,911,078 in other compensation, about $25.8 million in total.
Woods was reported at $16,507,215 plus $2,069,687 in other compensation as co-CEO in FY2023, meaning his reported pay rose roughly 39% in the first year she chaired the board.
HEA Consultants is a private LLC with no public financial disclosures.
lobbying: Advocate Health reported $2.02 million in in-house federal lobbying expenses for 2025 ($850,000, $380,000, $390,000 and $400,000 by quarter) and $1.87 million for the first three quarters of 2026, including $1.17 million in Q1 2026 alone.

Advocate also paid outside firms in 2025, including BGR Government Affairs ($320,000), Venable ($200,000) and McDermott+ ($120,000, under the Advocate Aurora name); Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center reported another $80,000.

Advocate's 2025 and 2026 lobbying reports list the 340B program, Medicaid funding, Medicare Advantage, site-neutral and hospital reimbursement policy, surprise billing and price transparency, and Stark Law and Anti-Kickback reform.
Advocate's in-house lobbying team includes Meagan Thompson, a former senior policy adviser to Rep. Robin Kelly and legislative assistant to Rep. Sean Casten.
No federal lobbying registration for HEA Consultants, LLC was found.
revolvingDoor: Chaired the board of Advocate Health through the post-merger integration of Advocate Aurora and Atrium.
Brings a professional-director and governance-consultant profile rather than a hospital operating role to the AHA board.
Joins the AHA Board of Trustees for a three-year term beginning Jan. 1, 2027.
homeSystemRecord: Advocate Health's charity care at cost was $148M (latest hospital tax returns).
Advocate Health has 859 340B contract pharmacy arrangements registered with HRSA (OPAIS registry, Sept. 29, 2026).
Advocate Health was formed by the December 2022 combination of Advocate Aurora Health and Atrium Health, creating one of the largest nonprofit systems in the country.
The AHA credits her with guiding Advocate's board through COVID-19, FTC proceedings and workforce challenges and with integrating the merged organizations' cultures.
Advocate lists the 340B program as a lobbying issue in every 2025 and 2026 quarterly federal report reviewed, signaling a material stake in the program's drug discounts.

Advocate now runs 69 hospitals and more than 1,000 sites of care in six states with about 167,000 employees, and CEO Eugene Woods credits the 2022 merger with $1.5 billion in annual operating savings.

Advocate's Atrium Health is taking over WakeMed in Raleigh: Wake County commissioners approved the deal 5-2 on September 21, 2026, with Atrium becoming sole member, funding $2 billion in capital and $150 million for a county health program, and capping rate increases at 1.5 times annual Medicare increases for only five years; it still needs North Carolina attorney general certification.
State Treasurer Brad Briner, who runs the state employee health plan, warned that the WakeMed deal would reduce competition and let the combined system negotiate higher prices.
litigation: Wisconsin residents filed a class action in February 2024 in the Eastern District of Wisconsin alleging Advocate Aurora used acquisitions, all-or-nothing contracting and anti-steering terms to raise commercial prices from 231% to 253% of Medicare; Advocate calls the suit meritless, and its current status was not verified.

In June 2026 Advocate Aurora reached a settlement to end a proposed class action in the Northern District of Illinois alleging it charged workers an unlawful tobacco surcharge through its employee health plan; terms were not disclosed.
Advocate Aurora paid $12.225 million to settle class claims that Meta Pixel tracking on its websites exposed patient data, a settlement approved during Baker Richardson's board tenure.

Atrium Health (then Carolinas HealthCare System) settled the U.S. Justice Department and North Carolina antitrust suit filed in 2016 over anti-steering contract terms, agreeing in 2018 to stop blocking insurers from steering patients to lower-cost rivals.
The AHA release references FTC proceedings during her board leadership without naming the matter.
redFlags: Advocate made a $4.6 billion bottom line in 2025, mostly from about $3 billion in investment income, while keeping tax-exempt status and lobbying to protect 340B program discounts.
Baker Richardson chaired the board that oversaw a reported $25.8 million package for CEO Eugene Woods in FY2024, a 39% jump from FY2023.
She has collected more than $880,000 in Advocate board fees from FY2018 through FY2024 as a director of a tax-exempt system.

Advocate Health spent about $2.7 million on federal lobbying in 2025 counting outside firms ($2.02 million in-house plus $640,000 to BGR, Venable and McDermott+), with the 340B program and site-neutral payment among its top issues.
Her AHA seat comes from her governance role at a mega-merger system, not from running a hospital, adding another voice for consolidated systems to the trade group's board.
She steered the board of a system built by a multistate mega-merger, the consolidation model that free-market critics say reduces competition and raises prices for employers and patients.

Advocate's Atrium unit is absorbing WakeMed with a price cap that expires after five years, over the state treasurer's warning that it will raise prices, and Advocate Aurora faces a pending Wisconsin antitrust class action alleging prices rose to 253% of Medicare.
patternSummary: Baker Richardson is a professional board director whose path to the AHA runs through chairing Advocate Health, the mega-system created by the Advocate Aurora-Atrium merger. Her board approved pay of roughly $25.8 million for its CEO, booked a $4.6 billion 2025 bottom line on investment gains and kept expanding, with Atrium now absorbing WakeMed over price warnings from North Carolina's treasurer, while facing an antitrust class action in Wisconsin. Her trustee seat adds a consolidation-era governance voice to an AHA board already dominated by large systems.

name: Kurt A. Barwis, FACHE
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Bristol Health in Bristol, Conn., since 2006. The system is anchored by 154-bed Bristol Hospital and includes EMS, the Ingraham Manor nursing home and a physician network.
AHA Board of Trustees member for a three-year term that began Jan. 1, 2024 and ends Dec. 31, 2026; he was not on the July 2026 slate of trustees elected for 2027.
Has served on the Connecticut governor's Healthcare Cabinet since 2016.

Former AHA Regional Policy Board 1 delegate (2019-2021) and 2017 recipient of the Connecticut Hospital Association's Grassroots Champion award, given for advocacy to repeal the state hospital tax and raise Medicaid rates.
Long-time Connecticut Hospital Association insider: CHA board member since 2007 and chair of the CHA CEO Forum since 2010.
Former ACHE Regent for Connecticut (2016-2019), later elected to the ACHE Board of Governors.
Named a 2026 Baldrige Foundation leadership award recipient ("Power 50") in April 2026.
Earlier roles: SVP and COO of St. Mary's Hospital (Maryland), system VP of managed care at Union Hospital (Maryland), and CFO of medical device startup Renaissance Technology.
financial: Barwis received $650,032 in reportable pay plus $37,738 in other compensation in FY2024 (year ended Sept. 30, 2024), according to Bristol Hospital Inc.'s Form 990.
His FY2023 pay was $676,472 plus $36,655 in other compensation, in the year auditors raised substantial doubt about the hospital's ability to continue as a going concern.

Bristol Hospital Inc. reported FY2024 total revenue of $175.2 million, expenses of $168.1 million and net income of $7.1 million, but ended the year with negative net assets of minus $32.0 million (liabilities of $138.0 million against assets of $106.0 million).
Connecticut's Office of Health Strategy put Bristol Hospital's operating margin at -4.7% in 2024, versus a statewide average of -2.3%, and at -10.2% in 2023.

Bristol posted a $637,017 operating gain in the first five months of FY2025, after two years of losses totaling more than $30 million, helped by eliminating 60 positions for about $3.5 million in annual savings.

In FY2022 Bristol breached a debt covenant on its $34.6 million 2019 bond issue, with 35 days of cash against a 45-day minimum. Cash fell to 16.89 days by May 31, 2023, and lawmakers pledged $7 million in state aid conditioned on a turnaround plan.
In January 2024, Barwis asked the community for $1 million in donations, which equaled about two days of cash on hand, so the hospital could meet bond covenants by September.
lobbying: No federal Lobbying Disclosure Act filings were found for Bristol Hospital or Bristol Health in 2025 or 2026.

Barwis has lobbied in Connecticut for years through the Connecticut Hospital Association, including a 2011 public clash with Gov. Dannel Malloy over a 5.5% provider tax and the 2017 campaign to repeal the hospital tax.
As a member of the governor's Healthcare Cabinet since 2016, Barwis sits inside the state policy apparatus that is now financing his hospital's rescue through UConn Health.

Connecticut lawmakers passed legislation in November 2025 clearing the way for state-owned UConn Health to acquire Bristol Hospital and Day Kimball Hospital. Bristol thanked the Lamont administration for its support.
revolvingDoor: Member of the Connecticut governor's Healthcare Cabinet since 2016.
He is handing his independent hospital to a state agency, UConn Health, after years on a state advisory body and in the hospital association that lobbies the state for money.
No federal government roles were found.
homeSystemRecord: On April 28, 2026, Bristol Health signed a non-binding letter of intent to join the state-owned UConn Health Community Network. Barwis said he expects the deal to close in December 2026 or January 2027, and no price or deal structure has been disclosed.

UConn Health Community System published notice in June 2026 that it would file a Certificate of Need application with the Office of Health Strategy to absorb Bristol Hospital and Day Kimball Hospital, listing an estimated capital expenditure of $0.

The acquirer is a taxpayer-backed academic system: a 2024 Cain Brothers report commissioned by the governor found UConn Health averaged $140 million a year in cash-flow losses from 2020 to 2023. UConn Health bought bankrupt Prospect's Waterbury Hospital in March 2026.
Bristol eliminated 60 administrative and clerical positions in 2024, about a third through layoffs, and cut overtime and administrator pay.

Nearly three-quarters of Bristol's patients had government insurance, versus a statewide average of 49% in fiscal 2021. Barwis says Medicare Advantage pays about 11% to 12% below traditional Medicare rates.

Earlier, Bristol proposed selling the 128-bed Ingraham Manor nursing home to for-profit operators for $10.5 million, and in 2014 it pursued an acquisition by for-profit Tenet Healthcare that did not close.
litigation: No federal enforcement actions, False Claims Act settlements, antitrust actions or state attorney general actions against Bristol Health in 2025 or 2026 were found.
The UConn Health takeover requires Connecticut Certificate of Need approval from the Office of Health Strategy, and that review was pending as of the latest reporting found.
Bristol's patient-debt lawsuit practices were not found in public reporting.
redFlags: A sitting AHA trustee's hospital is being rescued by the state. After a going-concern audit, a bond covenant breach and $30 million-plus in two-year losses, Bristol's exit strategy is acquisition by taxpayer-owned UConn Health.

The state-owned acquirer itself lost an average of $140 million a year from 2020 to 2023. Connecticut taxpayers are underwriting the consolidation of failing independent hospitals into a public system that also loses money.
Barwis took home about $688,000 in FY2024 and $713,000 in FY2023, while the hospital carried negative net assets of about $32 million and appealed to residents for donations to meet bond covenants.
Barwis sits on the governor's Healthcare Cabinet, and the governor's administration backed the UConn takeover of his hospital. That is an insider path to a state bailout.
No purchase price or deal terms have been disclosed six months after the letter of intent, and the public notice lists a capital expenditure of $0.
Barwis's CHA advocacy history consists of lobbying the state for more Medicaid money and lower hospital taxes. It is subsidy-seeking as the business model, ending in public ownership.
patternSummary: Barwis built his AHA seat through two decades of association work at CHA, ACHE and an AHA regional board, not institutional scale. His 154-bed hospital spent his AHA term in financial distress: a going-concern audit, a covenant breach, layoffs and negative net assets. The endgame is a state-financed takeover by money-losing UConn Health, backed by the same administration whose Healthcare Cabinet he sits on. His AHA term ends Dec. 31, 2026, about when Bristol expects to stop being an independent hospital.

name: Marc L. Boom, MD
title: President & CEO
affiliations: 2026 AHA Board Chair (Chair-Elect Designate 2024, Chair-Elect 2025), becoming Immediate Past Chair on January 1, 2027. As chair he helped select Steve Walsh to succeed Rick Pollack.
Has been President & CEO of Houston Methodist since 2012. Houston Methodist is an academic system anchored by its Texas Medical Center flagship, affiliated with Weill Cornell Medicine.
Sits on the board of directors of the Houston Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, for a three-year term that began in January 2024.
Past Chair (2021) of the Texas Hospital Association.
Member of the Vizient CEO Executive Board. Vizient is the nation's largest hospital group purchasing organization.
Past Chair (2023) of the Greater Houston Partnership; serves on the Houston advisory board of Amegy Bank (Zions Bancorporation).
Wrote the AHA 'Chair File' column and hosted the Leadership Dialogue series throughout 2026, covering advocacy, rural hospitals, AI and patient safety.
financial: FY2024 Form 990 for Methodist Hospital Group (filed November 7, 2025): Boom is listed by name with $7,251,200 in reportable compensation and $1,087,378 in other compensation, about $8.34 million in total.
That is up from about $7.14 million in total compensation on the FY2023 Methodist Hospital Group return.

Methodist Hospital Group FY2024: revenue of $4.40 billion, expenses of $3.93 billion, an excess of about $470 million, and net assets of $6.91 billion. FY2023 revenue was $3.93 billion with an excess of about $390 million.
The Methodist Hospital (flagship entity) FY2024: revenue of $3.60 billion, expenses of $3.28 billion, an excess of about $313 million, total assets of $11.86 billion and net assets of $8.46 billion.
The next-highest-paid executives named on the FY2024 group return were Kevin Burns ($2.93M), Roberta Schwartz, PhD ($2.77M) and Ramon Cantu ($2.47M).
The Lown Institute lists Houston Methodist Hospital with about $1.15 billion in real estate, property that is largely shielded from local property tax by its nonprofit status.
lobbying: Houston Methodist reported $200,000 in federal lobbying in 2024 and $200,000 in 2025, according to OpenSecrets. A 2026 year-to-date figure could not be confirmed.
Houston Methodist-affiliated individuals and PACs gave $203,937 in the 2024 cycle, according to OpenSecrets.
Houston Methodist Hospital is a registered lobbying client in Texas, active on Medicaid financing, property-tax exemption, scope of practice and surprise billing.
As 2026 AHA chair, Boom presided over an association that reported $25.47 million in federal lobbying in 2025 and $14.39 million in the first three quarters of 2026.
In an October 2026 AHA interview, Boom named 340B, site-neutral payment and mitigating the effects of the 2025 reconciliation law (OBBBA) as AHA's near-term fights.
revolvingDoor: His Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Houston Branch directorship (from January 2024) gives the CEO of one of Houston's largest employers a seat in the regional monetary-policy apparatus while he chairs the hospital lobby.
As 2026 AHA chair, he was the hospital industry's top elected officer in dealings with Congress, HHS and CMS during the fight over Medicaid cuts in the 2025 reconciliation law and over 340B rebates.
He was not among the members HHS/CMS named to its Healthcare Advisory Committee in March 2026; his successor as AHA chair, Bill Gassen, was.
homeSystemRecord: Houston Methodist Hospital received a D for equity on the Lown Institute Hospitals Index, ranking 3,724 of 3,764 hospitals nationally and 265 of 269 in Texas. Lown's fair-share analysis estimates a deficit of about $222 million, meaning the value of its tax exemption exceeds its spending on community investment.

Three Houston Methodist hospitals (Willowbrook, Baytown and West) take part in the 340B program. A 2022 FDLI analysis said acquiring outpatient sites let Methodist bill chemotherapy drugs through 340B, 'resulting in $50 million in profits to Methodist in one year alone.'
In a 2025 comment letter, Houston Methodist told CMS that combined 340B payment reductions 'would severely destabilize hospital operations.'

Rice University's Baker Institute found that Houston Methodist did not post prices for more than a year after the January 2021 federal transparency deadline, and later found major insurer rates missing from its file. Rice researchers reported continued extreme price variation in 2025.

Houston Methodist confirmed to KPRC 2 in 2024 that it charges facility fees at hospital-based outpatient clinics (transplant, wound care, radiation oncology, infusion), the practice site-neutral reform targets.

It has expanded mainly by building in affluent suburbs: the $650M+ Houston Methodist Cypress Hospital opened in March 2025, and a $247M expansion of Houston Methodist West was announced in August 2024.
litigation: Houston Methodist paid $9.99 million to settle DOJ False Claims Act allegations that it inflated charges in 2001-2003 to obtain improper Medicare outlier payments.

In October 2025, Texas AG Ken Paxton warned Boom that Houston Methodist might be violating HB 4076 by denying organ transplants to unvaccinated patients. The system denied having such a policy. No public enforcement action was found as of November 2026.

Houston Methodist is one of roughly 450 providers suing major insurers over alleged suppression of out-of-network rates through Claritev (formerly MultiPlan) in the Northern District of Illinois. DOJ filed a statement of interest backing plaintiffs in March 2025, and no trial is expected before 2027.

Bridges v. Houston Methodist: the suit by employees fired over the 2021 COVID-19 vaccine mandate was dismissed, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed. Fired staff were reported to be seeking Supreme Court review in January 2026, and the outcome could not be confirmed.
In 2022, ENT physician Mary Bowden sued Houston Methodist for $25 million, alleging defamation after the system publicly criticized her COVID-19 vaccine statements.
redFlags: The 2026 AHA chair took about $8.34 million in FY2024 pay from a nonprofit system that posted a $470 million surplus on $4.4 billion in revenue.

Lown ranks his flagship 3,724th of 3,764 on equity and estimates a roughly $222 million fair-share deficit. The tax exemption is worth more than what the system returns to the community, even while AHA tells Congress that nonprofits more than earn their exemption.
He reportedly made $50 million in one year from 340B by acquiring outpatient sites, then chaired the association suing to stop 340B rebates that would let manufacturers verify discounts.
Houston Methodist charges hospital facility fees at outpatient clinics while AHA, under his chairmanship, fought site-neutral payment that would end that markup.
His system ignored the federal price transparency rule for more than a year, later posted files missing major payer rates, and the association he chaired had sued to kill the rule.
Federal Reserve branch board seat: a hospital CEO with a seat in the regional monetary-policy apparatus while serving as the hospital lobby's chair.
Capital follows insured patients: hundreds of millions in new suburban capacity in Cypress, West Houston and The Woodlands while the urban flagship lags on community benefit.
patternSummary: Marc Boom runs a $4.4 billion nonprofit that posted a $470 million surplus and paid him about $8.34 million in FY2024, while Lown ranks his flagship near last in the country on equity and community benefit. As 2026 AHA chair, he led the fights to protect exactly the revenue streams his own system uses: 340B margins, facility fees and opaque pricing. He hands the gavel to Bill Gassen in January 2027 but stays on the AHA's executive leadership as Immediate Past Chair.

name: Joan Coffman, FACHE
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of St. Tammany Health System in Covington, La., operated by St. Tammany Parish Hospital Service District No. 1. She began her career there as a radiologic technologist in 1982.
AHA Board of Trustees: elected August 2024 to a three-year term that began Jan. 1, 2025 and runs through 2027; she is listed on the current AHA roster.
Chair of AHA Regional Policy Board 7, the Gulf South advisory body that feeds policy recommendations to the AHA board.
Board member of the Ochsner Health Network, the clinically integrated network of Louisiana's dominant health system.
Past chair of Vizient Southern States, a regional arm of the nation's largest hospital group purchasing organization.

Named chair-elect of the Louisiana Hospital Association board on July 20, 2026; she becomes LHA chair after the 2026-27 term, putting her at the head of the state hospital lobby while she sits on the AHA board.
Member of the Louisiana Committee of 100 for Economic Development since May 2024.
Previously led Hospital Sisters Health System hospitals in Illinois and Wisconsin.
financial: St. Tammany Health System is a parish hospital service district, a governmental entity that does not file IRS Form 990, so Coffman's pay and Schedule H charity care data are not in ProPublica or GuideStar.

Her pay does appear in the district's state-filed audit: the schedule of agency head compensation shows $802,091 salary, $195,000 retirement contribution, $21,174 insurance and a $9,000 car allowance, about $1.03 million in total, for both 2022 and 2023.

STHS reported $489.1 million in operating revenue and $41.9 million in operating income (an 8.6% margin) in 2023, up from $450.8 million and $43.0 million in 2022. Its net position grew 12% to $524.1 million, of which $436.8 million was unrestricted.
The district reported $6.4 million in federal grants as nonoperating revenue in 2023 and $1.1 million in 2022, alongside investment gains of $15.0 million.
Fitch affirmed STHS's AA- issuer default and bond ratings with a stable outlook in August 2024. No 2025 or 2026 rating action was found.

STHS markets itself as 'a self-sustaining nonprofit that accepts no taxpayer dollars,' a claim contradicted by its own audit (federal grants) and its federal lobbying for appropriations, and one that ignores the value of its tax exemption and governmental status.
lobbying: Senate LDA filings show St. Tammany Health System paid Adams and Reese LLP $120,000 in 2025 ($30,000 a quarter) and $90,000 through Q3 2026 to lobby Congress and the Executive Office of the President on one issue: 'Assist client in securing federal funding for the hospital.' The same firm separately lobbies for St. Tammany Parish government.

That corrects earlier research that found no federal lobbying registrations for STHS. The system it describes as accepting 'no taxpayer dollars' pays a lobbying firm specifically to win federal money.
As incoming LHA chair (chair-elect since July 2026), Coffman helps set the state hospital lobby's priorities on Medicaid payment and certificate-of-need (facility need review) policy.
The LHA has historically opposed loosening Louisiana's facility need review rules, which protect incumbent hospitals such as STHS from new competitors.
As RPB 7 chair and AHA trustee, she helps shape the federal agenda of the AHA, which leads opposition to site-neutral payment and defends 340B eligibility.
No personal federal political contributions by Coffman were identified.
revolvingDoor: Appointment to the Louisiana Committee of 100 gives her a seat in an invitation-only business group that advises state leaders on economic policy.
Her combined roles span federal policy (AHA trustee and RPB 7 chair), state lobbying (LHA chair-elect), group purchasing (Vizient) and commercial contracting (Ochsner network).
homeSystemRecord: Because STHS files no 990, there is no public Schedule H. Its audit reports charity care of only about $5.6 million in 2023 and $5.9 million in 2022, measured at full charges, roughly 1.1% of operating revenue. Bad debt was $23.9 million in 2023, about four times the charity figure.

Lown Institute's 2025 report found Louisiana nonprofit hospitals ran a combined fair-share deficit of $315 million a year (2020-2022), and community investment there averaged just 2.49% of expenses against a 5.36% tax-exemption value. Lown's study covers private nonprofits, so governmental districts like STHS fall outside it.

Its 340B eligibility flows from its governmental status, not from any demonstrated volume of care for the poor. In 2023 it bought Braswell's, a Covington retail pharmacy across from the flagship hospital, expanding its retail pharmacy footprint.
Net position grew $56.3 million in 2023, and the system holds more than $436 million in unrestricted net position.
No 2025 or 2026 strikes, closures, layoffs or credit downgrades were found in news or rating-agency coverage.
litigation: No 2025 or 2026 lawsuits, settlements or enforcement actions involving St. Tammany Health System were found in news coverage or federal audit records. Its federal single audits for 2022-2024 report no findings.
redFlags: She leads a governmental hospital district that escapes the Form 990 disclosure required of nearly every other nonprofit hospital, yet she helps govern the AHA, which defends nonprofit hospital tax exemption nationally.

Her roughly $1.03 million annual package is disclosed only in a state audit schedule, not in any federal filing, while the system reported charity care of about $5.6 million at full charges in 2023, around 1.1% of revenue.
The 'no taxpayer dollars' message is contradicted by $6.4 million in 2023 federal grants and by a lobbying contract whose sole stated purpose is securing federal funding for the hospital.
As incoming LHA chair she will lead the state hospital association that defends facility need review rules shielding STHS from competition.
She sits on the Ochsner Health Network board, and Ochsner CEO Pete November joined the AHA board on Jan. 1, 2026, giving the Ochsner orbit two Louisiana seats on the national board.
Her past chairmanship of Vizient Southern States ties her to a GPO whose vendor-fee model is not publicly transparent.
patternSummary: Coffman runs a public hospital district that claims nonprofit virtue and 'no taxpayer dollars' while taking federal grants, paying lobbyists to win federal funding, and avoiding the 990 disclosure that would put her roughly $1 million pay and its thin charity care in plain view. She has built governance seats across every lever of Gulf South hospital power: federal lobbying (AHA), state lobbying (incoming LHA chair), purchasing (Vizient), contracting (Ochsner's network) and economic policy (Committee of 100). With Ochsner's CEO now also on the AHA board, the Louisiana incumbents have a doubled voice in Washington.

name: Chris DeRienzo, MD
title: Senior Vice President and Chief Physician Executive, AHA; President, Health Research & Educational Trust
affiliations: Senior Vice President and Chief Physician Executive of the AHA since his appointment in December 2022, and President of the Health Research & Educational Trust (HRET); he remains on the Executive Management Group under CEO Steve Walsh as of November 2026.
Former System Chief Medical Officer and SVP of Quality at WakeMed Health & Hospitals in Raleigh, N.C., his role immediately before AHA.
Former Chief Quality Officer at Mission Health in Asheville, N.C.
Independent director on the board of Mednition, a clinical AI company selling to hospitals, since March 2024; Mednition is a portfolio company of the AHA Innovation Fund via Concord Health Partners.

Listed as an adviser to Concord Health Partners, the investment firm that manages the AHA Innovation Development Fund, and as Chief Medical Officer of Prealize Health, an AI predictive analytics company.
Former member of Premier Inc.'s board of advisors (through 2022).
MD from Duke University and MPP from Duke's Sanford School; board-certified in pediatrics and neonatology.
financial: DeRienzo's reportable 2024 compensation was $886,847 plus $174,720 in other compensation, about $1.06 million total, per AHA's 2024 Form 990.
His reportable pay was $829,789 in 2023, per Paddock Post.
The 2024 Form 990 shows him working about one hour a week for related organizations with no related-organization pay reported.
Compensation, if any, from his Mednition board seat or Concord Health Partners advisory role is not publicly disclosed.

AHA's 2024 Form 990 reports total revenue of $146.7 million against expenses of $169.3 million, a $22.6 million operating deficit, with net assets falling from $289.8 million to $277.6 million during the year.
Former CEO Rick Pollack's reportable 2024 compensation was $5,823,759 (plus $55,174 other compensation), up from $3,396,123 in 2023.
lobbying: DeRienzo is not a registered federal lobbyist on AHA's 2025 or 2026 LDA reports.

AHA's in-house LDA reports show $25.47 million in federal lobbying for 2025 (Q1 $7.03M, Q2 $6.15M, Q3 $5.72M, Q4 $6.57M); that total already includes about $1.68 million paid to outside lobbying firms.

AHA's 2026 in-house lobbying fell sharply during the CEO transition: $6.08 million in Q1, $4.47 million in Q2 and $3.84 million in Q3, or $14.39 million year to date, plus about $1.07 million to outside firms.

AHAPAC reported $3.49 million in receipts for the 2025-2026 cycle through Oct. 14, 2026, with $2.30 million in contributions to other committees, $1.26 million in independent expenditures, and cash on hand down to $683,005.

At a March 2026 House Energy & Commerce hearing, AHA CEO Pollack was the only one of six panelists to defend the ban on new physician-owned hospitals; no public statement by DeRienzo on that ban or on site-neutral payment has been found.
His public portfolio centers on clinical leadership, quality, physician well-being and AI, giving AHA a physician face while its lobbyists fight physician-owned competition.
revolvingDoor: Moves between hospital executive suites, AHA, and companies that sell to hospitals, including Mednition, which AHA's own innovation fund backs.
Concord Health Partners, where he is listed as an adviser, manages the AHA Innovation Development Fund that invested in Mednition, the company on whose board he sits.
No federal government service is publicly reported.
homeSystemRecord: As HRET president he heads AHA's research affiliate, which produces studies AHA cites in its advocacy.
AHA's 2024 Form 990 reports a $22.6 million operating deficit in a year his total pay rose to about $1.06 million.
AHA, via its innovation fund, holds investments in hospital vendors such as Mednition, mixing trade-association advocacy with venture returns from selling to members.
litigation: No personal litigation, malpractice action or enforcement matter involving DeRienzo has been publicly reported.

AHA's institutional litigation in 2025-2026 includes the successful D. Maine challenge to HRSA's 340B rebate pilot (injunction Dec. 29, 2025; pilot abandoned Feb. 5, 2026) and a new Oct. 9, 2026 suit against the revised pilot.
redFlags: He sits on the board of Mednition, a hospital-facing AI vendor backed by the AHA Innovation Fund, while serving as AHA's top physician executive, and any board compensation is undisclosed.
He is also listed as an adviser to Concord Health Partners, the manager of the same AHA innovation fund, creating a loop between his AHA role, the fund, and its portfolio company.
His title lends physician credibility to an association that defends the physician-owned hospital ban and fights site-neutral payment, yet he has made no public statement on either.
He runs HRET, AHA's research arm, so the physician who validates AHA's positions also controls the research pipeline used to support them.
He has never run an independent practice; his career has been inside hospital systems and the businesses that sell to them.
patternSummary: Chris DeRienzo is AHA's physician face and head of its research affiliate, paid about $1.06 million in 2024. He also sits on the board of Mednition, a hospital AI vendor backed by the AHA Innovation Fund, and is listed as an adviser to the fund's manager, Concord Health Partners. He talks about quality and physician well-being while AHA lobbies to keep physician-owned hospitals banned and facility fees intact, and he has stayed silent on both.

name: Eric D. Fish, MD, MBA, FACOG
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Schneck Medical Center in Seymour, Ind., since September 2020. He is also President of Health Development Corporation and Coordinated Health, both Schneck subsidiaries, and an ex officio member of the Schneck Medical Center Foundation board.
Elected to the AHA Board of Trustees on Sept. 9, 2025 to fill a vacancy through Dec. 31, 2026, then re-elected in July 2026 to a full three-year term beginning Jan. 1, 2027.
Chair of AHA Regional Policy Board 5.
Board member of the Indiana Hospital Association and Suburban Health Organization.
Board member of SIHO Holdings, a hospital-affiliated insurance entity, and of JC Bank, a local community bank.
Board member of the Jackson County Industrial Development Corporation, Community Foundation of Jackson County, Boys & Girls Club of Seymour and the Jackson County Ambulance Board.

Board-certified OB/GYN who joined Schneck in 2005, founded Schneck Obstetrics & Gynecology in 2006, and rose through Chief Medical Officer and COO to CEO. He holds an MD from Indiana University and an MBA from the University of Tennessee.
financial: Schneck is a county-owned hospital organized under Indiana Code 16-22. It does not file a standard Form 990, so Fish's compensation does not appear on ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer and was not found in any public source.
Schneck's audited FY2024 (calendar 2024) total operating revenue rose 7.5% to $392.8 million, against operating expenses of $379.5 million, for operating income of $13.3 million.
Schneck's net position rose $26.0 million in 2024 to $488.2 million, after a $28.9 million increase in 2023.
Schneck raised its rates 2% in 2024 after holding them flat in 2023.
Charity care was $1.87 million in charges and an estimated $913,352 in cost in 2024, about 0.23% of operating expenses, compared with $17.3 million written off as bad debt.

Schneck books revenue from 14 long-term care facilities it operates through lease and management arrangements. It recognized $19.9 million in nursing-home Medicaid upper payment limit (UPL) supplemental payments in 2024, up from $13.9 million in 2023, which exceeds its operating income.
Schneck carried a $16.3 million executive deferred compensation liability (including a 457(f) plan) at the end of 2024, up from $14.2 million.
Fish's executive pay may be spread across Schneck, Health Development Corporation, Coordinated Health and outside boards (SIHO Holdings, JC Bank), and no single public filing captures it.
lobbying: No federal Lobbying Disclosure Act filings for Schneck have been found since 2006, when MCapitol Management reported $30,000 in income from Schneck Memorial Hospital.
As an Indiana Hospital Association board member, Fish helps steer the state's main hospital lobby on hospital reimbursement, scope of practice, certificate of need and workforce issues.
As a continuing AHA trustee and chair of AHA Regional Policy Board 5, he helps shape the AHA's federal agenda, including its opposition to physician-owned hospitals.
revolvingDoor: Fish's governance seats concentrate in one county of about 44,000 people: the county hospital, a hospital-affiliated insurer (SIHO Holdings), the local bank (JC Bank), the county industrial development corporation and the ambulance board.
Schneck CFO Deborah Mann also sits on the SIHO Holdings board, which means two Schneck executives are on the board of an insurer that deals with the hospital.
No federal or state government roles were found.
homeSystemRecord: In 2024, Schneck added physicians in primary care, anesthesia, pain management, psychiatry, nephrology and general surgery. It also opened a Level II nursery and began a new electronic health record system set to go live in fall 2025.
Agency labor cost Schneck more than $5.4 million in 2024.

Auditors flagged a repeat significant deficiency in internal controls for 2024: cashiers could both take patient payments and post adjustments or write-offs to patient accounts. Management concluded the cost of fixing it outweighed the benefit.
The 2024 audit also flagged weak segregation of duties at Schneck's nursing homes.
Patients' own payments made up 4% of Schneck's gross revenue but 23% of its receivables at the end of 2024, which points to heavy self-pay collections.
Schneck had $15.8 million in Series 2020 revenue refunding bonds outstanding at the end of 2024, with covenants on days of cash, debt service coverage and debt-to-capitalization.
No 2025 or 2026 layoffs, strikes, closures, mergers or credit rating actions involving Schneck were found.
litigation: No False Claims Act, antitrust, state attorney general, or patient-debt litigation against Schneck Medical Center in 2025 or 2026 was found.
redFlags: Schneck's charity care cost was $913,352 in 2024, less than a quarter of one percent of its $379.5 million in operating expenses and about one-nineteenth of its $17.3 million in bad debt, while its net position grew $26 million.

Schneck's bottom line leans on government supplemental money. The $19.9 million in nursing-home UPL payments it recognized in 2024 exceeds its entire $13.3 million operating income, an arrangement that turns a county hospital into a pass-through for federal Medicaid dollars.

Auditors twice flagged that Schneck cashiers can both collect patient payments and write off patient balances. Management declined to fix it on cost grounds, at a hospital where 23% of receivables are owed by patients.

Fish now holds a full three-year AHA term starting in 2027 and chairs Regional Policy Board 5, which gives a small county hospital's CEO a vote on AHA positions, including its long-running opposition to physician-owned hospitals.

Fish's pay is not publicly disclosed. As a county hospital, Schneck files no Form 990, which leaves his compensation opaque despite public ownership. Schneck's $16.3 million executive deferred compensation liability is visible but not attributed to individuals.

Fish sits on the boards of the hospital, a hospital-affiliated insurer, the local bank and the county economic development corporation, a concentration of local governance seats that public filings do not police.
Schneck raised rates 2% in 2024 while sitting on $488 million in net position.
patternSummary: Fish is the physician who crossed fully to the institutional side. After a one-year fill-in seat, he has won a full AHA term starting in 2027, alongside an AHA regional policy board chair and a seat on the Indiana Hospital Association board. His county-owned hospital is profitable and asset-rich ($488 million in net position), but it provides token charity care and leans on Medicaid nursing-home supplemental payments that exceed its operating income. The county structure keeps his own pay off any public 990.

name: Christina (Tina) Freese Decker
title: President & CEO
affiliations: Served as 2025 AHA Board Chair and 2026 Immediate Past Chair. Her AHA officer cycle ends December 31, 2026, when Marc Boom moves into the past-chair seat.

President & CEO of Corewell Health since the 2022 Spectrum Health-Beaumont Health merger, and CEO of Spectrum Health from 2018 to 2022. Corewell is Michigan's largest system, with 21 hospitals, 300+ outpatient sites and about 60,000 employees.
Corewell owns Priority Health, a provider-sponsored health plan with 1.3 million+ members.
Board of Directors, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, for a three-year term from 2026 through 2028.

Board member of Business Leaders for Michigan and The Right Place (West Michigan economic development); former board member of the Michigan Health & Hospital Association and the American College of Healthcare Executives.
financial: Her Form 990 compensation was about $6.95 million in FY2024 ($5,453,830 reportable plus $1,498,970 other), up from about $6.73 million in FY2023 ($5,358,468 plus $1,373,681) and about $4.5 million in FY2022.

Schedule J breakdown (FY2024, the Corewell Health group return): base salary $2.49M, bonus and incentive $2.73M, other reportable $237,857, retirement and deferred $1.46M, nontaxable benefits $36,825; total $6.95M. Bonus and incentive pay was 39% of the total.
Paddock Post's review of the 2024 Corewell filing puts her cumulative compensation at about $31 million over 2018-2024.

Corewell's audited FY2025 results showed $17.6 billion in operating revenue ($9.8 billion patient revenue, $7.4 billion Priority Health premiums) and $276 million in operating income, a 1.6% margin, up from 1.3% in 2024.

Net income was $1.3 billion in 2025, driven by $1.1 billion in investment returns. The system held $9.9 billion in cash and investments (214 days cash on hand) and $12.5 billion in net assets at year-end 2025.
Corewell's top 64 executives received about $65 million in total compensation in 2023.
Former Beaumont CEO John Fox received a reported $10.2 million departure package after the merger.
lobbying: Corewell Health's in-house LDA filings report $830,000 in federal lobbying for 2025 ($190,000, $270,000, $190,000 and $180,000 by quarter), up from $620,000 in 2024 LDA filings, and $590,000 for the first three quarters of 2026.

Its 2025-2026 filings list 340B ('covered entities and manufacturer created barriers (Lilly)'), PBM reform, Medicare Advantage star-ratings recalculation, Medicaid financing, tariffs, physician visa fee exemptions and NIH appropriations.
Corewell-affiliated PACs and individuals contributed $420,461 in the 2024 cycle, per OpenSecrets.
As 2025 AHA chair she fronted the association's opposition to site-neutral payment and Medicaid cuts and its defense of 340B. That year AHA reported $25.47 million in federal lobbying.
Corewell's pharmacy business services director has testified before Michigan lawmakers in defense of the 340B program.
revolvingDoor: She has spent her whole career inside Spectrum/Corewell since a 2002 administrative fellowship, with no government service.

Her Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago directorship (2026-2028) gives the CEO of Michigan's largest employer-insurer-provider a seat in the regional monetary-policy apparatus, mirroring Boom's Dallas Fed seat.
She chaired Spectrum Health's price transparency and quality transparency task forces (2016-2020) before leading the trade group that had sued to block the federal hospital price transparency rule.
homeSystemRecord: Corewell Health's charity care at cost was $54.1M (latest hospital tax returns).
Corewell Health has 995 340B contract pharmacy arrangements registered with HRSA (OPAIS registry, Sept. 29, 2026).

The $13 billion Spectrum-Beaumont cross-market merger drew an FTC second request but was allowed to close in 2022. Michigan AG Dana Nessel extracted no conditions on Beaumont's roughly $4 billion in reserves, and her office said the deal fell outside its authority.

Through vertical integration, Corewell runs the state's largest hospital network and the Priority Health plan. The PriorityIntegra narrow-network product, launched January 2025, steers members to Corewell providers.

In Lown Institute's 2025 analysis, Michigan nonprofit hospitals had a combined fair-share deficit of about $605 million a year (2020-2022), 75% of hospitals ran deficits, and community investment equaled just 1.76% of expenses, the lowest of the 20 states studied. Beaumont's eight metro Detroit hospitals alone ran a $165 million deficit on 2021 data.

About 10,000 Teamsters-represented nurses at Corewell Health East (former Beaumont) voted about 90% in March 2026 to authorize a strike. No strike occurred: a tentative agreement was reached July 29, 2026, and the nurses ratified a three-year first contract in August 2026 with 15% raises over its term, a lump sum for a previously withheld raise and a safe-staffing committee, but no fixed nurse-to-patient ratios.

In 2025, Corewell cut about 186 billing and finance jobs and moved the work offshore to India, according to Deadline Detroit. This followed about 400 management and non-clinical layoffs after the merger in 2022.
Two 2023 data breaches exposed the information of more than 1 million Michigan patients, which AG Nessel publicly announced.
litigation: Rzanca et al. v. Corewell Health et al. (E.D. Mich., No. 2:26-cv-11692), filed May 22, 2026: a proposed class action alleging Corewell and debt collector DCM Services sought to collect millions of dollars in medical bills that had already been paid through insurance and government programs.
A False Claims Act case, Collins v. Corewell Health, was filed in the Western District of Michigan in 2026 (No. 1:26-cv-00324). Its allegations and status were not public as of November 2026.

Before the merger, William Beaumont Hospital paid $84.5 million to settle False Claims Act allegations of improper financial relationships with eight referring physicians (Anti-Kickback and Stark laws, 2004-2012).
Beaumont was among the Detroit-area hospitals that paid a combined $42 million by 2015 to settle claims that they conspired to suppress nurse wages.
Teamsters Local 2024 filed unfair labor practice charges against Corewell Health East during the 2025-2026 first-contract fight, which ended with an August 2026 ratified contract.
A former physician filed a Whistleblower Protection Act suit in 2023 alleging opioid overprescribing and religious discrimination at a Corewell clinic in Taylor, Michigan.
redFlags: CEO pay reached about $6.95 million in FY2024, about $31 million cumulative over 2018-2024, while the system withheld nurse raises and premium pay until 10,000 nurses authorized a strike.

Corewell posted a 1.6% operating margin in 2025 but $1.3 billion in net income and $9.9 billion in cash and investments, which undercuts the hospital-lobby claim of financial distress that she pressed as AHA chair.
A May 2026 class action alleges Corewell pursued patients for medical debts already paid by insurers and government programs.
Through vertical integration Corewell owns the dominant hospital network and the health plan that pays it, with a narrow-network product that locks members into Corewell providers.

The cross-market megamerger closed with no AG conditions on Beaumont's roughly $4 billion in reserves. The FTC second request produced nothing, and cross-market deals remain a blind spot in antitrust enforcement.
It inherited an $84.5 million kickback settlement and a $42 million nurse wage-fixing settlement from Beaumont, and a new False Claims Act case was filed against Corewell in 2026.
Michigan hospitals have the lowest community-investment rate among the 20 states in Lown's 2025 study, and the state's largest system was led by the 2025 AHA chair.
She sits on the Chicago Fed board while serving as past chair of the hospital lobby, the same pattern as Boom at the Dallas Fed.
patternSummary: Tina Freese Decker built Corewell through Michigan's largest cross-market merger, creating a $17.6 billion vertically integrated system that controls both the state's biggest hospital network and a major health plan, with no state conditions on the $4 billion in reserves it absorbed. She chaired the AHA in 2025, its record lobbying year, pleading hospital distress while Corewell booked $1.3 billion in net income and her pay hit about $6.95 million. Her AHA officer cycle ends December 31, 2026, but she keeps her Chicago Fed seat through 2028.

name: Gerald "J.P." Gallagher
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President & CEO of Endeavor Health (Evanston, IL) since the 2022 NorthShore/Edward-Elmhurst merger; previously President & CEO of NorthShore University HealthSystem (2017-2022), NorthShore COO, and President of Evanston Hospital.

Named president and CEO-designate of the combined Rush-Endeavor system announced October 14, 2026: 12 hospitals, 400+ care sites, 46,000+ employees and nearly $11 billion in revenue, operating under the Rush brand.

Member of the Madison Dearborn Partners Healthcare Advisory Council, a private equity firm's healthcare advisory body.

Member of the Civic Committee of the Commercial Club of Chicago, Young Presidents Organization, Chicago Health Executives Forum and the Northwell CEO Council on gun violence prevention; previously listed on the Healthcare Leadership Council.
Board Chair of the Gallagher Foundation, his family's scholarship foundation; Fellow of the American College of Healthcare Executives.
Princeton University (BA) and Wharton School (MBA); early career at The Lewin Group and Advocate Health Care's Christ Medical Center.
financial: Gallagher's total reported compensation was $5,191,626 in 2024 on the Form 990 of Endeavor Health Clinical Operations (formerly NorthShore University HealthSystem), including roughly $2.1 million base salary and $1.4 million bonus.
His reported pay was $6,283,529 in 2023, and roughly $24 million cumulatively from 2017 through 2023 per Form 990 analysis.
The 37 highest-paid employees on the 2024 Endeavor Health Clinical Operations 990 received about $47 million combined; that filing entity alone reported $2.3 billion in revenue.
