Endeavor booked $62.3 million in legal settlement costs in 2025 after $457.2 million in 2024, the latter including $453 million tied to sexual abuse claims against former gynecologist Fabio Ortega.
Despite the operating loss, Endeavor posted 2025 net income of $663.3 million on investment returns, and is pledging a $1 billion investment from its endowment as part of the Rush merger.
S&P affirmed Endeavor's 'AA-' rating with a stable outlook in May 2024 when it priced $291 million in Illinois Finance Authority refunding bonds.
lobbying: No 2025 or 2026 federal lobbying filings are registered under the Endeavor Health or NorthShore names in the Senate LDA database; Endeavor's federal advocacy runs through the AHA and the Illinois Health and Hospital Association.
Merger partner Rush University System for Health paid Cozen O'Connor Public Strategies $120,000 for federal lobbying in 2025 and $90,000 through Q3 2026.
The AHA, on whose board Gallagher sits, reported $25.47 million in federal lobbying expenses in 2025 and $14.39 million in the first three quarters of 2026.
Gallagher chaired the Illinois Health and Hospital Association in 2023, the state trade group that lobbies on Medicaid rates, tax exemption and certificate-of-need policy in Springfield.

Illinois maintains a certificate-of-need regime; in March 2025 the state review board blocked Endeavor's plan to end inpatient psychiatric care at Northwest Community Hospital, showing the same incumbent-protection system can also bind the incumbent.
revolvingDoor: No federal or state government positions found for Gallagher.
Sits on the Madison Dearborn Partners Healthcare Advisory Council, linking a nonprofit system CEO to a private equity firm's healthcare deal flow.
Past chair of the Illinois Health and Hospital Association and current AHA trustee, giving him leadership roles in both the state and national hospital lobbies.
homeSystemRecord: Endeavor and Rush announced a merger on October 14, 2026 that would create a 12-hospital, roughly $11 billion system in northern Illinois and northwest Indiana; the deal is targeted to close in early 2027, subject to regulatory review.

Evanston Hospital, Endeavor's flagship, had the largest fair-share deficit in Illinois at -$152 million per year (2020-2022 average) in Lown Institute data: about $198 million in tax exemption value against $47 million in community investment.

Endeavor planned to cut about 100 jobs and end inpatient psychiatric services at Northwest Community Hospital in Arlington Heights in April 2025; the state review board blocked the closure plan on March 19, 2025.
Endeavor said in January 2025 it would eliminate up to roughly 100 positions after a $127 million net loss in the first nine months of 2024.

Nearly 3,000 nurses at Evanston, Skokie, Glenbrook and Highland Park hospitals began organizing with Teamsters Local 743 in spring 2026, citing pay cuts of $5 to $22 an hour and understaffing; two Evanston ICU nurses were fired in May 2026.
Teamsters Local 743 filed an NLRB election petition on October 22, 2026 for about 2,408 registered nurses; Endeavor moved to postpone the hearing and on November 2, 2026 filed a motion to dismiss.
Rush nurses voted to unionize with National Nurses United in 2026, and Edward Hospital nurses in Naperville have petitioned for an election, setting up the merged system to face two nurse unions.
litigation: Endeavor paid $453 million in 2024 to settle civil claims by former patients of gynecologist Fabio Ortega, who pleaded guilty in 2021; by April 2024 at least 60 former patients had sued Ortega, Endeavor and/or Swedish Hospital.
Endeavor recorded a further $62.3 million in legal settlement costs in 2025; the matters covered have not been publicly itemized.

In January 2024 Endeavor agreed to pay $55 million to settle a consumer class action alleging NorthShore used market power from its 2000 acquisition of Highland Park Hospital to inflate prices; the FTC had earlier found that merger anticompetitive.

Four nurses sued Endeavor in federal court in Illinois on August 15, 2025 (No. 1:25-cv-09768) alleging unpaid pre- and post-shift work and interrupted meal breaks under the FLSA and Illinois wage laws; one plaintiff also alleges she was fired after a manager searched her phone over union talk. No resolution has been reported.

At least three unfair labor practice charges were filed against Endeavor with the NLRB between March and June 2026 alleging retaliation and surveillance of organizing nurses, per a June 2, 2026 letter from Rep. Jesus "Chuy" Garcia to Gallagher.
The FTC and Illinois Attorney General sued in December 2015 to block the NorthShore-Advocate merger, and the parties abandoned the deal.
redFlags: Gallagher's NorthShore, whose 2000 Highland Park acquisition was found anticompetitive and cost $55 million to settle in 2024, is now set to have him run a roughly $11 billion merged Rush-Endeavor system in the same Chicago market.
Endeavor's flagship Evanston Hospital has the largest fair-share deficit in Illinois at -$152 million per year, receiving about four times more in tax breaks than it returns in community investment.
Gallagher was paid $6.28 million in 2023 and $5.19 million in 2024 while Endeavor ran operating losses, cut jobs, and sought to close a behavioral health unit.
Endeavor's $453 million Ortega abuse settlement is among the largest of its kind by a US hospital system and covers abuse alleged over decades at hospitals now in Endeavor's system.
Endeavor is fighting a nurse union drive at four NorthShore hospitals: two nurses fired, at least three NLRB charges, a congressman's letter, and a motion to dismiss the Teamsters' election petition.
Endeavor posted $663 million in 2025 net income and is committing $1 billion of endowment money to a merger, while nurses report pay cuts and the system lost money on operations.
A pending federal wage suit alleges Endeavor deliberately understaffed nurses to cut costs, forcing unpaid overtime.
patternSummary: Gallagher is a career consolidator. NorthShore's Highland Park merger was found anticompetitive, regulators blocked its Advocate merger, the Edward-Elmhurst deal created Endeavor, and now Rush. Each step builds market leverage in Chicagoland, while the flagship hospital takes in roughly four times more in tax breaks than it returns and Gallagher collects $5 million to $6 million a year. The 2026 nurse union fight and the Ortega settlement show a system that protects the institution first.

name: Bill Gassen
title: President & CEO
affiliations: Becomes 2027 AHA Board Chair on January 1, 2027. He was named Chair-Elect Designate in July 2025 and served as Chair-Elect in 2026.

President & CEO of Sanford Health since November 2020. After the January 1, 2025 Marshfield Clinic Health System combination and the September 1, 2026 merger with Minneapolis-based North Memorial Health, Sanford spans the Dakotas, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Nebraska with roughly 56,000+ employees.
Appointed in March 2026 as one of 18 members of the HHS/CMS Healthcare Advisory Committee, which advises the HHS Secretary and CMS Administrator on Medicare, Medicaid and CHIP.
Chairs the Coalition to Strengthen America's Healthcare, the AHA-founded 501(c)(4) advocacy and ad campaign group that opposes Medicare and Medicaid cuts.
Has sat on the board of Oscar Health, Inc. (NYSE: OSCR), a publicly traded health insurer, since December 2022.
Board member of Medical Alley and the Greater Sioux Falls Chamber of Commerce. He is a lawyer who was Sanford corporate counsel (from 2012) and chief human resources officer before becoming CEO.
financial: His Form 990 compensation rose to about $5.0 million in FY2024 ($4,414,119 reportable plus $585,241 other), up from about $3.26 million in FY2023 ($2,821,352 plus $439,680), a 53% one-year jump. FY2022 was about $3.06 million and FY2021 about $3.35 million.

Schedule J breakdown (FY2024, the Sanford Group Return): base salary $2.33M, bonus and incentive $1.62M, other reportable $455,266, retirement and deferred $584,349, nontaxable benefits $892; total $5.00M. Bonus and incentive pay was 32% of the total.
The Sanford parent return (EIN 45-3791176) reported $6.11 billion in revenue and $281 million in net income for FY2024, after $5.74 billion in revenue and $365 million in net income in FY2023.

Systemwide audited FY2025 results, the first year including Marshfield, showed $11.7 billion in operating revenue but only $210.9 million in operating income, a 1.8% margin, down from 5.2% in 2024. Net income still reached $1.1 billion on investment and nonoperating gains.
His 53% raise in FY2024 came the year before the system's operating margin fell by more than two-thirds.

Former CEO Kelby Krabbenhoft collected about $49.5 million on his November 2020 exit ($15 million severance, $29.4 million retirement payouts, $5.1 million salary). That was part of about $65 million paid to six departing executives in one year.
As an Oscar Health director, Gassen receives board compensation from an insurer whose rates and networks depend on negotiations with hospital systems like his own.
lobbying: Senate LDA filings under the client name Sanford Health show $720,000 in outside-firm lobbying in 2025 (Bockorny Group $400,000; Chamber Hill Strategies $320,000) and $540,000 for the first three quarters of 2026. OpenSecrets, which can aggregate affiliates differently, previously put Sanford at $560,000 (2020), $910,000 (2022) and $960,000 (2024).
Marshfield Clinic Health System, now part of Sanford, files its own LDA reports: $240,000 in 2025 and $180,000 through Q3 2026. Combined Sanford-family federal lobbying was about $960,000 in 2025.

Sanford's 2025-2026 filings list Medicare reimbursement rates, Medicaid reform, budget reconciliation, across-the-board spending cuts, federal hospital funding, rural health and immigration as lobbying issues.
Sanford-affiliated PACs and individuals contributed $246,174 in the 2024 cycle, per OpenSecrets.

As chair of the Coalition to Strengthen America's Healthcare, he heads a 501(c)(4) that is not required to disclose donors. In 2025 it ran national TV and digital ads and generated more than 575,000 letters to Congress against Medicare and Medicaid cuts.
As 2027 chair he takes over an AHA that reported $25.47 million in federal lobbying in 2025, then cut spending 24% in the first three quarters of 2026.
revolvingDoor: In March 2026 he joined the HHS/CMS Healthcare Advisory Committee while serving as AHA Chair-Elect, so the incoming head of the hospital lobby is formally advising the agency that sets hospital payment rates.
At the same time he chairs the AHA's 501(c)(4) issue-advocacy arm and sits on a publicly traded insurer's board (Oscar Health).
From January 2027 he will hold the AHA chair and a federal advisory seat at the same time, an unusual concentration of industry, lobbying and regulatory-advisory roles in one person.
homeSystemRecord: Sanford Health's charity care at cost was $89.1M (latest hospital tax returns).
Sanford Health has 458 340B contract pharmacy arrangements registered with HRSA (OPAIS registry, Sept. 29, 2026).

Sanford completed its merger with North Memorial Health (Robbinsdale and Maple Grove hospitals, Minneapolis suburbs) on September 1, 2026. Minnesota AG Keith Ellison approved it under a 10-year oversight agreement that includes a $600 million capital commitment, the first major test of the merger-review law Minnesota passed after Sanford's failed Fairview bid.

Sanford's merger record: it completed MeritCare (2009); the FTC and North Dakota AG blocked Mid Dakota Clinic (2017), with the court accepting that the deal would create 75-85% shares in Bismarck-Mandan physician services; talks with UnityPoint (2019) and Intermountain (2020) collapsed; and Fairview/M Health (2023) was abandoned after a Minnesota AG investigation.

The Marshfield Clinic Health System combination closed January 1, 2025, taking Sanford into Wisconsin. Prairie Lakes Healthcare (Watertown, SD) and the Lewis Drug retail pharmacy chain were also acquired.

In April 2025 Sanford laid off about 96 leadership and administrative employees as part of the Marshfield integration, while pledging $500 million of investment in the Marshfield region over five years.
The FTC found Sanford and Mid Dakota Clinic were 'each other's closest rivals' and that the merger would likely raise reimbursement rates and premiums.

Sanford participates in 340B across eligible hospitals, a Sanford pharmacy executive was elected to the 340B Health board in 2021, and Sanford considered but declined converting critical access hospitals to rural emergency hospitals partly because of the potential loss of 340B discounts. The Lewis Drug acquisition gives it a retail pharmacy network to run contract-pharmacy and in-house dispensing.

Lown Institute's 2025 fair-share report does not cover the Dakotas, so no hospital-level figure exists for Sanford's core market. The states Sanford has expanded into run large statewide deficits: Minnesota $487 million, Wisconsin $493 million and Iowa $162 million a year (2020-2022 averages).
litigation: Hanson v. Sanford Health (D. Minn., No. 25-cv-03129): a proposed class action alleging Sanford embedded Meta and other tracking pixels on its website and disclosed patients' data. On September 4, 2026, Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz denied dismissal of the federal Electronic Communications Privacy Act and Minnesota deceptive trade practices claims, so the case proceeds.

Former Sanford surgical oncologist Dr. Sabha Ganai alleges she was fired in retaliation for raising patient-safety concerns. The suit was filed in Cass County, N.D., in July 2024 under the state whistleblower law and has moved to federal court with discrimination and FMLA claims. It was pending as of March 2026.

Sanford Health, Sanford Medical Center and Sanford Clinic paid $20.25 million to settle False Claims Act allegations of Anti-Kickback violations and medically unnecessary spinal surgeries tied to neurosurgeon Wilson Asfora's physician-owned distributorship. Whistleblowers received $3.4 million, and Sanford entered a Corporate Integrity Agreement with HHS-OIG.
The whistleblower complaint alleged that Sanford leadership got 'numerous warnings' about the scheme. Sanford had earlier paid $625,000 to resolve kickback allegations involving the same surgeon.
FTC and State of North Dakota v. Sanford Health (2017): a federal court enjoined the Mid Dakota Clinic acquisition, and the Eighth Circuit affirmed.

Minnesota AG Keith Ellison investigated the proposed Sanford-Fairview merger in 2022-2023 under antitrust and nonprofit-asset law, received 3,500+ public comments and asked that closing be delayed. The deal was abandoned in 2023.
redFlags: Concurrent capture: from January 2027 he holds the AHA chair, chairs the AHA's dark-money-capable 501(c)(4), sits on a federal CMS/HHS advisory committee and holds an insurer board seat.
His pay rose 53% in one year, to about $5.0 million in FY2024, and the next year Sanford's operating margin fell from 5.2% to 1.8%.

Serial consolidation: one deal blocked by the FTC as a near-monopoly, one abandoned under state AG scrutiny that prompted a new merger-review law, then Marshfield (2025) and North Memorial (2026), which pushed Sanford into the Twin Cities under a 10-year AG oversight agreement.

The $20.25 million False Claims Act settlement and Corporate Integrity Agreement followed alleged repeated warnings to leadership about a surgeon's kickback scheme, after Sanford had already paid to settle similar allegations about the same surgeon.
A federal judge let a patient-privacy class action proceed in September 2026 over Sanford's alleged sharing of patient web data with Meta.
About $65 million in executive exit payouts in one year at a nonprofit, including about $49.5 million to a CEO forced out over his COVID-era conduct.

Sanford kept its namesake and donor relationship with T. Denny Sanford, whose fortune came from subprime credit cards, after ProPublica reported in 2020 that he was under investigation. No charges were filed.
patternSummary: Bill Gassen is a corporate lawyer turned CEO who has grown Sanford past $11.7 billion in revenue by absorbing Marshfield in 2025 and North Memorial in 2026, after regulators blocked or derailed two earlier deals. His own pay rose 53% to about $5 million in FY2024, the year before Sanford's operating margin collapsed to 1.8%. In January 2027 he becomes AHA chair while also sitting on HHS/CMS's federal advisory committee, chairing the AHA's 501(c)(4) and serving on an insurer's board. That puts the hospital lobby's top officer inside the agency that sets its rates.

name: Leah M. Glasgo
title: Market President
affiliations: Market President of UnityPoint Health-Fort Dodge since January 2019, running Trinity Regional Medical Center and the system's Fort Dodge market in north-central Iowa; also interim president of UnityPoint Health-Sioux City from 2021 to 2024.
Elected to the AHA Board of Trustees for a three-year term starting January 1, 2026; previously served on AHA Regional Policy Board 6.
Board of Directors member of the Iowa Hospital Association, the state hospital lobby.

Previously President & CEO of Stewart Memorial Community Hospital in Lake City, Iowa, for six years; joined UnityPoint in 2013 as VP of Rural Development, then VP of Clinical Operations and COO in Sioux City.
Local boards include the Fort Dodge Betterment Association, Fort Dodge Growth Alliance and Athletics for Education and Success.
Registered nurse since 1997; BSN from University of Nebraska Medical Center, MHA from Des Moines University (named its 2026 College of Health Sciences Alumna of the Year); FACHE.
financial: Glasgo was paid $602,275 in 2024 ($508,390 reportable plus $93,885 other compensation), all from related organizations, according to Trinity Regional Medical Center's Form 990.

Her pay peaked at about $1.17 million in 2022 ($1,067,658 plus $100,798) and was about $981,000 in 2023 while she also ran the Sioux City market; it fell about 39% in 2024 after the interim role ended.

Trinity Regional Medical Center (Fort Dodge) reported $206.0 million in revenue, $187.9 million in expenses and $18.1 million in net income for 2024, with $224.7 million in net assets and $29.7 million in liabilities.
Revenue at the Fort Dodge hospital has grown about 60% since 2018, from $128.8 million to $206.0 million in 2024.

Parent filer Iowa Health System (UnityPoint Health) reported a $51.4 million deficit on $442.4 million revenue in 2024 and negative net assets of $56.0 million at the parent level; its 990 discloses first-class or charter travel for executives.
UnityPoint's parent 990 for 2024 lists CEO Scott Kizer at about $2.37 million and former CEO Clay Holderman, who left in October 2023, at about $1.55 million.
Fort Dodge is building a $39.8 million surgery renovation and expansion due to open in March 2027, with $10 million committed by the Trinity Foundation.
lobbying: UnityPoint Health reported $240,000 in in-house federal lobbying in 2025 ($60,000 per quarter) and $180,000 through Q3 2026, covering the 340B program, Medicare Advantage, rural health, telehealth and reimbursement.

In Q3 2026 UnityPoint hired Cozen O'Connor Public Strategies ($20,000 that quarter) to lobby on Medicare, Medicaid, the 340B program and safety-net issues; the lobbyist is Rodney Whitlock, former health policy director for Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa).
Glasgo sits on the Iowa Hospital Association board, which lobbies the Iowa legislature on Medicaid reimbursement, workforce and rural hospital funding.
The AHA reported $25.47 million in federal lobbying in 2025 and $14.39 million through Q3 2026; on the board, Glasgo is positioned as its rural voice.
revolvingDoor: No government positions found for Glasgo.

UnityPoint's new outside lobbyist, Rodney Whitlock, was a senior health aide to Sen. Chuck Grassley and the Senate Finance Committee, a direct line from Iowa's senior senator's office to UnityPoint's 340B and Medicare agenda.
Glasgo moved from AHA Regional Policy Board 6 to the national Board of Trustees in 2026, the standard pipeline for executives from member systems.
homeSystemRecord: Iowa hospitals had a combined fair-share deficit of -$162 million per year in the Lown Institute's 2020-2022 data; 70% of Iowa nonprofit hospitals received more in tax breaks than they spent on community investment. Fort Dodge's hospital-specific figure was not published in the report.

UnityPoint announced in April 2026 it would eliminate 207 IT roles, and confirmed on July 8, 2026 that it is outsourcing revenue cycle work to Omega Healthcare, citing sustained financial pressure; it says the revenue cycle cuts affect under 1% of its 31,000-person workforce.

Trinity Health sold MercyOne Siouxland Medical Center's operating assets in Sioux City to UnityPoint on September 1, 2025 for $3.5 million in cash, consolidating hospital competition in the market Glasgo ran on an interim basis from 2021 to 2024.

litigation: No 2025 or 2026 lawsuits, settlements, False Claims Act cases or state AG actions naming Glasgo or UnityPoint Health-Fort Dodge were found in available sources.
Trinity Regional Medical Center's Form 990 checks the box for reported conflict-of-interest transactions (Schedule L); details were not reviewed.
redFlags: Glasgo was paid $602,275 in 2024 and about $1.17 million in 2022 to run a rural market of roughly $200 million in revenue, all routed through related UnityPoint organizations rather than the hospital that lists her as an officer.

UnityPoint absorbed Sioux City competitor MercyOne Siouxland for $3.5 million in September 2025 after it lost $91.2 million under Trinity Health in fiscal 2025, leaving Sioux City with fewer competing hospital systems.
Trinity Regional posted an $18.1 million surplus in 2024 and holds $224.7 million in net assets, while 70% of Iowa nonprofit hospitals ran fair-share deficits.
UnityPoint hired a former Grassley health aide to lobby on the 340B program and Medicare in 2026, the same year it cut 207 IT jobs and outsourced revenue cycle staff.

patternSummary: Glasgo is the AHA board's rural nurse-turned-executive, used to make the rural hospital case to Congress. The 990s show a system-level executive paid $600,000 to $1.17 million a year to run a profitable regional hub, while UnityPoint consolidates competitors, outsources back-office jobs and hires a Grassley alum to protect the 340B program and Medicare money. The rural framing obscures a hub-and-spoke system whose strategy is scale.

name: Chad Golder
title: General Counsel and Secretary
affiliations: General Counsel and Secretary of the AHA since January 2024 (listed on the 2024 Form 990 as SVP, General Counsel & Secretary), succeeding Melinda Hatton; previously Deputy General Counsel. He remains on the Executive Management Group under CEO Steve Walsh as of November 2026.
Former partner and founding member of Munger, Tolles & Olson's Washington office, opened in 2016 with former U.S. Solicitor General Donald Verrilli.

Former senior Justice Department official, including Deputy Associate Attorney General and Counsel to the Deputy Attorney General in the Obama administration, working on ACA litigation among other matters.
Former Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia.
Former law clerk to Justice John Paul Stevens and to Judge Merrick Garland on the D.C. Circuit.
financial: Golder's reportable 2024 compensation in his first year as General Counsel was $1,070,865 plus $154,122 in other compensation, about $1.22 million total, per AHA's 2024 Form 990.
That is up from $797,836 in 2023 as Deputy General Counsel, per Paddock Post, a raise of roughly 34% in reportable pay on promotion.
His predecessor Melinda Hatton received $297,327 in 2024 reportable compensation after her role ended in December 2023.

AHA's 2024 Form 990 reports total revenue of $146.7 million against expenses of $169.3 million, a $22.6 million operating deficit, with net assets falling from $289.8 million to $277.6 million during the year.
Former CEO Rick Pollack's reportable 2024 compensation was $5,823,759 (plus $55,174 other compensation), up from $3,396,123 in 2023.
Senior executives at AHA receive taxable benefit allowances (SVPs and above) and access to a supplemental non-qualified deferred compensation plan, per the 2023 Form 990.
lobbying: Golder is not a registered federal lobbyist on AHA's 2025 or 2026 LDA reports; his tool is litigation against HHS, CMS and HRSA.

AHA's in-house LDA reports show $25.47 million in federal lobbying for 2025 (Q1 $7.03M, Q2 $6.15M, Q3 $5.72M, Q4 $6.57M); that total already includes about $1.68 million paid to outside lobbying firms.

AHA's 2026 in-house lobbying fell sharply during the CEO transition: $6.08 million in Q1, $4.47 million in Q2 and $3.84 million in Q3, or $14.39 million year to date, plus about $1.07 million to outside firms.

AHAPAC reported $3.49 million in receipts for the 2025-2026 cycle through Oct. 14, 2026, with $2.30 million in contributions to other committees, $1.26 million in independent expenditures, and cash on hand down to $683,005.
revolvingDoor: DOJ to BigLaw to trade association: he defended federal agencies' authority at DOJ, then went to an elite firm's government-facing DC office, and now runs a legal shop that sues the same agencies.
His Munger Tolles DC office was built around Obama-era Solicitor General Donald Verrilli.
No current government advisory roles or outside corporate board seats are publicly reported.
homeSystemRecord: Under Golder, AHA won the most consequential hospital-side court fight of 2025-2026: the Dec. 29, 2025 injunction that killed HRSA's first 340B rebate pilot.

AHA filed an amicus brief on June 17, 2026 in the 5th Circuit supporting Texas against HHS and CMS on Medicaid provider-tax 'hold harmless' rules, defending a state financing mechanism critics say inflates federal Medicaid matching dollars.

Before his tenure, AHA lost its challenge to the CMS price transparency rule at district court and on appeal in 2020, and lost its site-neutral case when the D.C. Circuit reversed its win and the Supreme Court declined review in 2021.
AHA won AHA v. Becerra unanimously at the Supreme Court in 2022, restoring 340B reimbursement rates.
litigation: 340B rebate pilot (AHA, Maine Hospital Association and four safety-net systems v. HHS, D. Maine): preliminary injunction granted Dec. 29, 2025; 1st Circuit denied stay Jan. 7, 2026; government dropped appeal Jan. 20, 2026; HHS told the court Feb. 5, 2026 it would vacate the pilot.

Revised 340B rebate pilot: AHA and co-plaintiffs sued again Oct. 9, 2026 in D. Maine to stop the revised pilot set for Jan. 1, 2027; on Oct. 21, 2026 AHA asked the court to deny intervention motions by drug companies and PhRMA. Pending.
Texas v. HHS (5th Cir.): AHA, CHA, AAMC and FAH filed an amicus brief June 17, 2026 urging affirmance of a ruling that vacated parts of CMS's 2023 provider-tax bulletin and 2024 managed care rule.
Site-neutral (AHA v. Azar): AHA's 2019 district court win was reversed by the D.C. Circuit in 2020 and the Supreme Court declined review in 2021; this matter is closed, not an active front.
No bar discipline or personal litigation involving Golder has been publicly reported.
redFlags: He uses DOJ-honed knowledge of how agencies defend rules to block them on behalf of hospitals, most effectively against 340B rebate reforms aimed at tracking how the discount is used.
AHA's courtroom strategy on the 340B program is to keep the discount flowing upfront and to stop rebate mechanisms that would expose claims data, protecting hospital spread revenue.
AHA's legal shop backs state provider-tax schemes in the 5th Circuit, which recycle federal Medicaid money through hospital taxes.
His pay jumped about 34% on promotion to roughly $1.22 million all-in for 2024, a year AHA ran a $22.6 million deficit.
The two biggest legal fights AHA lost on the merits, price transparency and site-neutral payment, were both efforts to keep hospital prices hidden and facility-fee markups intact.
patternSummary: Chad Golder is the AHA's chief litigator, a former senior DOJ lawyer and Munger Tolles partner who now sues HHS on the hospital lobby's behalf. On his watch AHA killed HRSA's first 340B rebate pilot in court and is back in the District of Maine to stop the revised version due Jan. 1, 2027. His promotion brought a roughly 34% raise to about $1.22 million in 2024, in a year AHA lost $22.6 million.

name: Charles Gressle

lobbying: HCA and its outside firms reported about $5.4 million in federal lobbying for 2025 in Senate LDA filings, including $4.15 million in-house plus Alston & Bird, Smith-Free Group, Mehlman Consulting, Rubin Turnbull & Associates and Hance Scarborough.
HCA reported about $5.17 million in federal lobbying in the first three quarters of 2026, including $4.15 million in-house, already near its full-year 2025 total.

HCA runs a federal PAC, the HCA Healthcare Good Government Fund; full 2025-2026 cycle totals were not verified for this dossier.
HCA joins an AHA board whose lobbying defends tax-exempt hospital privileges such as the 340B program, which HCA's for-profit hospitals largely do not share.
revolvingDoor: No government employment is publicly reported for Gressle; his career has been inside HCA.
His seat on AHA Regional Policy Board 4 already gave him a role in shaping AHA's Southeast policy positions before his trustee election.
homeSystemRecord: HCA's East Florida Division covers hospitals in the Fort Lauderdale, Miami and Palm Beach markets, including HCA Florida JFK in Atlantis.

In February 2026 nurse Leelamma Lal sued HCA Florida Palms West Hospital in Palm Beach County, HCA and security contractor Allied Universal, alleging negligent security after a Baker Act patient beat her on February 18, 2025; the complaint cites a history of violence at the hospital, and HCA says two regulators found no deficiencies.

HCA's federal lobbying reached about $5.17 million in the first nine months of 2026, close to its 2025 total of $5.4 million.

Quality reporting on HCA's South Florida hospitals has shown low CMS star ratings and state sanctions at HCA Florida JFK.
