Her 2024 package of about $1.99 million rose in a deficit year, and her public message on affordability points at everyone in health care except hospitals.

name: William M. Jennings
title: Senior Vice President, Hartford HealthCare; President, Fairfield Region
affiliations: Senior vice president of Hartford HealthCare and president of its Fairfield Region since July 19, 2021, overseeing St. Vincent's Medical Center in Bridgeport.
Previously executive vice president of Tower Health in Pennsylvania and president and CEO of its flagship 714-bed Reading Hospital.
Before Tower, spent eight years as CEO of Bridgeport Hospital and executive vice president of Yale New Haven Health, St. Vincent's main crosstown competitor.

Earlier served as president of SSM St. Mary's Health Center and the SSM St. Louis Heart Institute, and held executive posts at BayCare Health System in Florida and Cookeville Regional Medical Center in Tennessee.
Serves on AHA Regional Policy Board 1.
Bachelor's from Miami University (Ohio) and a Master of Hospital Administration from The Ohio State University.
Elected an AHA trustee in July 2026 for a three-year term beginning January 1, 2027.
financial: Hartford HealthCare reported $7.13 billion in operating revenue for fiscal 2025, with seven hospitals and about 48,000 employees before adding Manchester and Rockville.
SVMC Holdings, the St. Vincent's Medical Center parent he oversees, reported $616.3 million in revenue and $637.9 million in expenses on its tax year 2023 Form 990, a deficit of about $21.7 million.
St. Vincent's expenses exceeded revenue in each of the three most recent years with extracted 990 data: by $20.3 million in 2021, $35.2 million in 2022 and $21.7 million in 2023.
Hartford Hospital, the system's flagship, reported $2.58 billion in revenue and $2.46 billion in expenses on its tax year 2023 Form 990.

Jennings's pay is reported on the Form 990 of SVMC Holdings (St. Vincent's Medical Center, EIN 83-2550272), where he is listed as president and director but is paid entirely by a related Hartford HealthCare organization: $1,474,125 plus $191,193 in other compensation (about $1.67M) for the fiscal year ending September 2024, up from $1,433,652 plus $156,125 (about $1.59M) in FY2023 and $425,715 plus $66,898 in FY2022.
Hartford Hospital's revenue grew from $2.14 billion in tax year 2021 to $2.58 billion in tax year 2023 while St. Vincent's kept running deficits.

Hartford HealthCare paid $86.1 million to buy Manchester Memorial and Rockville General hospitals out of Prospect Medical Holdings' bankruptcy, closing January 1, 2026, and committed about $227 million in capital over three years.
lobbying: No 2025 or 2026 federal lobbying filings under the client name Hartford HealthCare appear in the Senate LDA database, though the system has registered as a federal lobbying client in earlier years.

Hartford HealthCare's state lobbying in Connecticut and any PAC activity were not verified for this dossier; the system is a major participant in Connecticut's certificate-of-need process, which approved its Manchester Memorial acquisition in December 2025.
revolvingDoor: No government employment is publicly reported for Jennings.

He moved directly from running Bridgeport Hospital for Yale New Haven Health to later running its main local rival, St. Vincent's, for Hartford HealthCare, an example of executives moving between competing systems in the same small market.
homeSystemRecord: St. Vincent's Medical Center posted operating deficits in every year with available 990 data (2021-2023), the period covering the start of Jennings's tenure.
Bridgeport's two acute care hospitals, St. Vincent's and Yale's Bridgeport Hospital, are each controlled by one of Connecticut's two dominant systems, leaving the city with no independent hospital.

Connecticut's Office of Health Strategy approved the Manchester Memorial acquisition on December 10, 2025, with conditions that tie commercial rate growth to the state cost growth benchmark and CPI-U medical index, require separate rate negotiation for Manchester, and bar converting physician offices to hospital-based billing for three years.
No charity care, price transparency or 340B program data specific to the Fairfield Region were verified for this dossier.
litigation: Saint Francis Hospital (Trinity Health Of New England) sued Hartford HealthCare in federal court in January 2022, alleging it monopolized Hartford County through physician practice acquisitions and referral control; the case was dismissed with prejudice in January 2025 after a confidential settlement.

Seven insured Connecticut residents are suing Hartford HealthCare in Hartford Superior Court under the state antitrust and unfair trade practices acts, alleging all-or-nothing contracting and anti-tiering and anti-steering clauses raised prices; the state attorney general filed an amicus brief backing their standing in 2023, and a class certification hearing was set for September 14, 2026.

Estuary Transit District and the Teamsters 671 health plan filed a putative federal class action in June 2024 (D. Conn., No. 3:24-cv-01051) alleging monopolization and price fixing since at least June 2020, including anti-steering clauses and de facto exclusive physician deals through Integrated Care Partners; in April 2026 plaintiffs moved to compel 182 documents Hartford HealthCare withheld as privileged.
Hartford HealthCare denies the antitrust allegations in all three cases.
No lawsuits or enforcement actions naming Jennings personally or the Fairfield Region in 2025 or 2026 were found.
redFlags: St. Vincent's, the hospital Jennings runs, has spent more than it took in every year with available 990 data, about $77 million in combined deficits over 2021-2023.
Jennings has led both sides of Bridgeport's two-system hospital market, first for Yale New Haven Health and now for Hartford HealthCare.

Jennings's employer faces two pending antitrust suits, one federal and one in state court, accusing it of using must-have hospitals, anti-steering clauses and captive physician networks to inflate commercial prices in Connecticut; a third, by rival Saint Francis, ended in a confidential settlement in 2025.

Hartford HealthCare kept growing by acquisition, buying Manchester Memorial and Rockville General for $86.1 million in January 2026, with regulators imposing rate-growth caps that underline the pricing concerns.
He is paid about $1.67 million a year through a related Hartford HealthCare entity rather than the hospital he runs, so his pay never shows up as an expense of St. Vincent's itself.
patternSummary: William Jennings is a career hospital executive who has run both of Bridgeport's hospitals for the two systems that control Connecticut's market, first Yale's Bridgeport Hospital and since 2021 Hartford HealthCare's St. Vincent's, which ran about $77 million in deficits over 2021-2023. His employer, a $7.13 billion system, faces pending federal and state antitrust suits over anti-steering and all-or-nothing contracting and settled a rival's monopolization suit in 2025, even as it bought two more hospitals in January 2026. He joins the AHA board in 2027 as a regional executive of a consolidating system whose market power is being litigated.

name: J. Stephen Jones, MD
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Inova Health in Fairfax/Falls Church, Va., since April 2018.
Former president of Cleveland Clinic Regional Hospitals and Family Health Centers and former Cleveland Clinic urology department chair.
Board-certified urological surgeon who still practices; professor of urology at the University of Virginia.
Former board chair of the American Medical Group Association and former editor of an American Urological Association journal.
Board member of the Economic Club of Washington, D.C., and the Greater Washington Partnership.
MD and BS from the University of Arkansas; MBA from Case Western Reserve University; Fellow of the American College of Surgeons.
Named to Virginia Business's 2026 Virginia Power 50 list; 2025 recipient of the Joint Commission's Award of Excellence.
financial: Jones received $6,505,967 in reportable compensation plus $73,484 in other compensation on Inova Health Care Services' FY2024 Form 990, up from $5,480,396 in FY2023 (an 18.7% raise in one year).
His reported pay has risen 69% in four years, from $3,845,532 in FY2020 to $6,505,967 in FY2024.
Inova Health Care Services reported FY2024 revenue of $6.42 billion, expenses of $6.01 billion and net income of $409.2 million on its Form 990.
For calendar 2025, Inova reported $7.3 billion in operating revenue (up 11.5%), $582.7 million in operating income and an 8.0% operating margin, up from 5.6% in 2024.
Inova's 2025 net income was $2.0 billion, up from $1.3 billion in 2024, roughly 3.4 times its operating income.
Inova booked $49.7 million in FEMA Public Assistance funding in 2025 tied to the COVID-19 emergency, a federal subsidy landing in a year it posted $2 billion in net income.
Five Inova executives and physicians other than Jones each received roughly $1.96 million to $2.35 million in FY2024 reportable compensation.
lobbying: No federal Lobbying Disclosure Act filings were found under Inova client names for 2024, 2025 or 2026; Inova's last outside federal lobbying registrations on record date to 2013-2014 (Squire Patton Boggs), so its federal advocacy runs largely through trade groups such as the AHA.
Jones gave $1,500 to the American Hospital Association PAC in August 2021 and again in September 2022, listing Inova Health System as his employer.
Jones gave $1,000 to AMGA Voice, the American Medical Group Association's PAC, in November 2021.

In Virginia, Inova registered in-house lobbyist Michael Forehand (VP, Government Relations) and retained lobbyist Myles Louria of Hunton Andrews Kurth for May 2026-April 2027, with stated issues including Medicaid, health insurance, certificate of public need (COPN), workforce and the state budget.

At a June 16, 2026 roundtable, Jones pressed Fairfax County to streamline its development process, saying 'If it's not doable to build, building doesn't happen,' while Inova separately lobbies Richmond on COPN, the state permission-slip regime that limits new competing facilities.
revolvingDoor: Serves on the AHA's Healthcare Advisory Council to the FBI.
Sits on the boards of the Economic Club of Washington, D.C., and the Greater Washington Partnership, two of the region's most influential business-policy networks.
Former board chair of the American Medical Group Association, a national trade group for large medical groups.
Joins the AHA Board of Trustees for a three-year term beginning Jan. 1, 2027.
homeSystemRecord: Inova runs five hospitals (Alexandria, Fairfax, Fair Oaks, Loudoun and Mount Vernon) with 1,840 licensed beds and more than 26,000 employees, making it the Washington region's largest private employer.
Inova reported $193 million in charity care and $338 million in total community investment for 2025, meaning charity care equaled about 2.6% of operating revenue.

A May 2025 Inova presentation on presumptive financial assistance showed $41.8 million in 2024 charity adjustments, equal to 0.17% of total charges against an internal goal of 3.5%; the slide labels the figures 'for presentation purposes only.'
Jones said in June 2026 that Inova's charity care rose 27% over the prior year.

Inova is building two new hospitals, a 192-bed hospital at the former Landmark Mall site in Alexandria and a 110-bed hospital in Franconia-Springfield, at a combined cost of roughly $2 billion to $2.5 billion, both targeted to open in late 2028.
Inova Alexandria Hospital on Seminary Road will close once the new hospitals open, with Inova exploring housing-focused redevelopment of the site.
Inova is doubling the Inova Fairfax Hospital emergency department, whose first phase of a $161 million expansion opened in late 2024; a second phase is expected to finish in 2028.
Inova launched its first comprehensive fundraising campaign in 2024 with a $500 million goal by Dec. 31, 2029.
litigation: In Lugo v. Inova Health Care Services (E.D. Va., filed April 29, 2024), patients alleged Inova's website tracking pixels sent MyChart users' health information to Meta and Google without consent.

Inova agreed to a $3,147,390 class settlement plus website compliance changes; the court granted preliminary approval Dec. 17, 2025, claims were due April 6, 2026, and a final approval hearing was set for April 16, 2026. The final approval ruling was not confirmed in available sources.
redFlags: Jones's pay hit $6.5 million in FY2024, up 69% since FY2020, at a tax-exempt system.
Inova posted $2.0 billion in 2025 net income and an 8.0% operating margin while still collecting $49.7 million in FEMA COVID-era aid.
Charity care of $193 million in 2025 was about 2.6% of a $7.3 billion revenue base, small relative to the value of Inova's tax exemption in one of the wealthiest regions in the country.
An internal 2025 presentation showed charity adjustments at 0.17% of charges against Inova's own 3.5% goal.
Jones demands faster permitting for Inova's own building program while Inova lobbies on Virginia's COPN law, which shields incumbents like Inova from new competitors.

Inova will close its Seminary Road Alexandria hospital as it shifts capacity to new facilities, consolidating capacity in Northern Virginia, where it is already the region's largest system and largest private employer.
Inova paid $3.1 million to settle claims that it leaked MyChart patients' health data to Meta and Google through tracking pixels.
No federal lobbying disclosures under Inova's name since 2014 means its Washington influence flows through the AHA, whose board Jones now joins.
patternSummary: Jones is a surgeon-turned-system builder who has turned Inova into the dominant, cash-rich hospital monopoly of Northern Virginia, posting $2 billion in 2025 net income while his own pay climbed to $6.5 million. Inova's charity care remains a low single-digit share of revenue, and the system pairs calls for easier permitting for itself with lobbying on a COPN regime that protects incumbents. His AHA seat gives the nation's wealthiest suburban market a direct voice at the trade group that does Inova's federal lobbying.

name: Laura S. Kaiser
title: President & CEO
affiliations: She has been President & CEO of SSM Health, the St. Louis-based Catholic system, since 2017. SSM has more than 40,000 employees, 24 hospitals, more than 540 physician offices and outpatient sites and 11 post-acute facilities across Missouri, Illinois, Wisconsin and Oklahoma.

The AHA board named her Chair-elect Designate on July 12, 2026. She will be Chair-elect in 2027 and AHA Board Chair in 2028. She already sits on the AHA Executive Committee and chairs the AHA Operations Committee.

She has been an independent director of Merit Medical Systems, a publicly traded maker of medical devices, since May 2022, serving on its Governance & Sustainability and Compensation & Talent Development committees. She was earlier a director of Nuance Communications (2017-2022).
She chairs the board of Navitus Health Solutions, a pharmacy benefit manager. SSM Health reports PBM revenue as a line of its business.
She chaired the Catholic Health Association board of trustees from July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2023. She is a former director of Joint Commission Resources, the Joint Commission's consulting affiliate.
She also sits on the boards of Greater St. Louis Inc. and the Seton Shrine National Leaders Council.

Before SSM she was EVP & COO of Intermountain Healthcare. Earlier, at Ascension, she was regional executive for the Gulf Coast/Florida region and President & CEO of Sacred Heart Health System in Pensacola.
financial: Her 2024 compensation, reported on the Form 990 of SSM affiliate SSM Audrain Health Care, was $5,205,665 from related organizations plus $2,681,148 in other compensation, about $7.89 million in total.

Schedule J breakdown (FY2024, SSM Health Care Corporation and four related returns): base salary $2.16M, bonus and incentive $2.24M, other reportable $803,415, retirement and deferred $2.66M, nontaxable benefits $24,591; total $7.89M. Bonus and incentive pay was 28% of the total.

Her total pay was about $1.59 million in 2017, $2.73 million in 2018, $4.18 million in 2019, $5.18 million in 2020, $5.70 million in 2021, $8.38 million in 2022, $7.65 million in 2023 and $7.89 million in 2024: roughly $43 million over eight years.
Her 2024 pay of about $7.89 million came in a year SSM Health posted a $70 million operating loss (-0.6% margin).

SSM Health's 2025 results: total operating revenue of $12.7 billion (up from $11.4 billion), operating income of $148.5 million (1.2% margin) and net income of $483.6 million, nearly double 2024's $249.3 million.

SSM's 2025 revenue included $2.6 billion in pharmacy benefit manager revenue, up from $2.2 billion. That is about one-fifth of the system's top line, on top of $7.3 billion in net patient service revenue.
Other 2024 SSM executive pay included Steven Smoot at about $3.48 million total and Douglas Long at about $2.29 million total.
lobbying: SSM Health hired Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath as its federal lobbying firm effective January 20, 2022, on Medicare graduate medical education, COVID provider relief, health equity and behavioral health. The firm's lobbyists include former aides to Reps. Chris Smith, Glenn Grothman and Susie Lee and Sen. Maria Cantwell.

In Wisconsin, SSM Health authorized lobbyist Alex Ignatowski on January 14, 2025 for the 2025-2026 session, on Medicaid reimbursement, postpartum Medicaid coverage, licensure compacts, the health care workforce and APRN scope of practice.
As AHA chair in 2028, she will lead the board of an association that reported $25.47 million in federal lobbying in 2025.
revolvingDoor: She serves on the board of a publicly traded medical device maker (Merit Medical) while running a health system that buys medical devices and while moving up the AHA chair line.
She chairs a pharmacy benefit manager's board (Navitus) while AHA attacks PBMs and insurers for squeezing hospitals.
She is a past chair of the Catholic Health Association, the lobbying and advocacy arm for Catholic systems on tax exemption and the 340B program.
No government service is publicly reported.
homeSystemRecord: SSM Health's charity care at cost was $68.1M (latest hospital tax returns).
SSM Health has 1,128 340B contract pharmacy arrangements registered with HRSA (OPAIS registry, Sept. 29, 2026).
SSM swung from a $70 million operating loss in 2024 to $148.5 million in operating income in 2025, with net income of $483.6 million.

In her first year, 2017, SSM laid off 350 employees (about 1% of its workforce) to ensure 'long-term sustainability.' In April 2020 it furloughed about 2,000 employees, roughly 5% of staff, for 13 weeks.

In 2018 SSM agreed to sell three rural Missouri hospitals (St. Mary's-Jefferson City and St. Mary's-Audrain to MU Health Care, St. Francis-Maryville to Mosaic). In 2020 it ended trauma, complex cardiac and neuro surgery and labor and delivery at SSM Health St. Joseph Hospital in St. Charles, Mo.
In 2023 SSM signed a 10-year partnership with Siemens Healthineers, a medical equipment vendor.
litigation: In Doe v. SSM Health Care Corporation, a Missouri class action filed December 5, 2022, SSM is accused of sending MyChart patients' health information to Meta and other third parties without consent. The settlement got preliminary approval September 2, 2025, offering $31.50 per claimant plus identity protection, with a final approval hearing November 21, 2025.

SSM Health and partner Navvis settled a class action over a July 2023 ransomware breach for $6.5 million without admitting wrongdoing (St. Louis Circuit Court, No. 2422-CC00208-01). The final approval hearing was July 10, 2025.
redFlags: Her pay rose from about $1.6 million in 2017 to about $7.9 million in 2024, and was $7.9 million in a year SSM lost $70 million on operations.
Her compensation is reported through related organizations on an affiliate's 990 (SSM Audrain) rather than on a systemwide parent filing, which makes it harder to trace.
About $2.6 billion of SSM's revenue comes from a pharmacy benefit business, and she chairs a PBM's board while AHA lobbies against PBM and insurer practices.
She holds a public-company board seat at medical device maker Merit Medical while running a system that buys devices.
SSM settled a Meta-pixel privacy class action and a $6.5 million ransomware breach class action in 2025.
SSM has cut rural and community services (three Missouri hospital sales in 2018, trauma and obstetrics cuts in St. Charles in 2020) while paying its CEO more than $5 million a year since 2020.
patternSummary: Laura Kaiser runs SSM Health, a $12.7 billion Catholic system that now books a fifth of its revenue from a pharmacy benefit business, and she is in line to chair the AHA in 2028. Her pay rose nearly fivefold to about $7.9 million in 2024, a money-losing year for SSM, and she holds outside board seats at a device maker and a PBM. She is a Catholic Health Association veteran and AHA insider who embodies the vertically integrated, tax-exempt conglomerate the AHA defends.

name: Vicki Lewis, FACHE
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Coffee Regional Medical Center (CRMC), a 98-bed nonprofit acute care hospital in Douglas, Ga., since 2014.
Chair of the Georgia Hospital Association Board of Trustees, installed July 9, 2026, after serving as chair-elect from 2025; GHA board member since 2019.
Former CEO and executive roles at Aurora Health Care (Milwaukee) and OhioHealth (Columbus).
BSN from Ohio University and MS from The Ohio State University; Fellow of the American College of Healthcare Executives.
2024 AHA Partnership for Action Grassroots Champion, one of 50 honorees nationally.
financial: Lewis received $742,392 in reportable compensation plus $19,533 in other compensation on CRMC's FY2024 Form 990, up 18.5% from $626,686 in FY2023.
Her reported pay has risen 90% since FY2018 ($391,313), while CRMC revenue grew about 50% over the same period ($132.9 million to $199.9 million).
CRMC reported FY2024 revenue of $199.9 million, expenses of $193.2 million and net income of $6.8 million (about a 3.4% margin), with net assets of $49.4 million.
CRMC's FY2023 Form 990 showed revenue of $187.3 million and net income of $2.9 million.
CRMC's FY2021 federal single audit, filed with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse, reported a material weakness in internal controls.

Contributions to CRMC peaked at $14.1 million (7.4% of revenue) in FY2021; CRMC actively solicits gifts through Georgia's HEART rural hospital tax credit, which refunds donors 100% of their gift as a state income tax credit, up to a $100 million statewide cap per year.
lobbying: No federal Lobbying Disclosure Act filings were found for Coffee Regional Medical Center in 2024, 2025 or 2026.

As Georgia Hospital Association chair, Lewis leads a group that has retained Cornerstone Government Affairs for federal lobbying since at least 2025, reporting $40,000 per quarter (about $120,000 for Q2-Q4 2025 and $120,000 for Q1-Q3 2026).
The AHA honored Lewis in 2024 as a Grassroots Champion for educating elected officials on hospital priorities; the award materials did not name specific legislators or bills.
CRMC promotes Georgia HEART, a state program that converts private donations into dollar-for-dollar tax credits for rural hospitals, effectively redirecting state tax revenue to hospitals like hers.
revolvingDoor: Served on AHA Regional Policy Board 4 (AHA dates it 2022-2025; CRMC dates it 2021-2024) and will chair the AHA Region 4 Policy Board.
Chairs the Georgia Hospital Association board from July 2026, the state's main hospital lobby.
Joins the AHA Board of Trustees for a three-year term beginning Jan. 1, 2027, as the board's rural independent hospital voice.
homeSystemRecord: CRMC has served Coffee County and surrounding counties since 1953 and operates as an independent nonprofit hospital.
Under Lewis, CRMC launched an internal medicine residency program and expanded outpatient services across the region.
CRMC has earned national accreditations in cancer care, interventional cardiology and stroke readiness, and promotes bariatric, orthopedic and spine service lines.

CRMC returned to profitability after FY2017 ($6.5 million loss) and FY2018 ($2.9 million loss) and has posted surpluses every year from FY2019 through FY2024, ranging from $1.1 million (FY2020) to $10.9 million (FY2021).

CRMC has been enrolled in the 340B program as a disproportionate share hospital (ID DSH110089) since April 1, 2007, with three registered child sites (Coffee Regional First Care, an outpatient infusion center and a wound care clinic).

HRSA's 340B database lists seven active contract pharmacy arrangements for CRMC, including a Walmart pharmacy and independent pharmacies in Douglas and Nicholls; a second Walmart arrangement in Hazlehurst and an earlier Nicholls contract were terminated in 2018.
No Lown fair-share ranking or price transparency compliance data for CRMC was found.
litigation: No lawsuits, settlements, False Claims Act actions or state AG actions involving Coffee Regional Medical Center in 2025 or 2026 were found in available sources; local coverage through September 2026 was limited to service-line, residency and scholarship announcements.
redFlags: Lewis's pay rose 90% from FY2018 to FY2024, outpacing the hospital's 50% revenue growth, at a 98-bed rural hospital that leans on taxpayer-backed donations.
CRMC solicits donations through Georgia HEART, a 100% state tax credit program that is a direct subsidy routed through private donors.
CRMC has drawn 340B program discounts since 2007 and routes them through seven active contract pharmacies, including Walmart, giving Lewis a direct stake in the 340B fight the AHA leads.
CRMC's FY2021 federal single audit reported a material weakness in internal controls.
Lewis now chairs the Georgia Hospital Association, which pays an outside federal lobbying firm $40,000 a quarter, and will sit on the AHA board, stacking state and national trade-group roles.
She was named an AHA Grassroots Champion for lobbying elected officials, a sign she is valued for advocacy as much as operations.
patternSummary: Lewis is the AHA board's rural community-hospital face, a nurse-trained executive who has run a 98-bed Georgia hospital since 2014 while climbing the Georgia Hospital Association and AHA advocacy ladder. Her pay has risen far faster than her hospital's revenue, and CRMC relies in part on Georgia's dollar-for-dollar HEART tax credit to raise money. Her seat gives the AHA a sympathetic rural story to tell in Washington, even as the trade group's agenda is driven by large systems.

name: Pete November
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Ochsner Health since November 2022, succeeding Warner Thomas; previously Ochsner's executive vice president of digital health, chief financial officer and chief administrative officer.
Elected by AHA in November 2025 to fill a board vacancy for a term running January 1, 2026 through December 31, 2028.

Board member and Treasurer of the National World War II Museum; also sits on the Business Council of New Orleans and the River Region, the Committee of 100 and the University of Kentucky Visiting Committee.
Certified public accountant with a bachelor's in accounting and a law degree from the University of Kentucky.
Adjunct professor at the University of Queensland College of Medicine and adjunct professor and guest lecturer at Loyola University New Orleans College of Business.
Named to Modern Healthcare's 100 Most Influential People in Healthcare.
financial: November was paid $6,112,385 in reportable compensation plus $899,128 in other compensation by Ochsner Clinic Foundation in FY2024, per its Form 990.

Schedule J breakdown (FY2024, Ochsner Clinic Foundation): base salary $2.08M, bonus and incentive $3.91M, other reportable $120,102, retirement and deferred $866,860, nontaxable benefits $32,268; total $7.01M. Bonus and incentive pay was 56% of the total.
His reportable pay rose from $4,183,651 in FY2023 to $6,112,385 in FY2024, a 46% one-year increase, and has roughly tripled from $1,936,112 in FY2020.
He was not the highest-paid person at Ochsner in FY2024: Benjamin Peeler, MD was paid $6,742,839; Ochsner reported $41.1 million in total executive compensation that year.
Predecessor Warner Thomas was paid $10,003,805 in his final year (2022) before leaving Ochsner in November 2022.
Ochsner Clinic Foundation's FY2024 Form 990 shows $6.04 billion in revenue, $5.71 billion in expenses and $325.1 million in net income, up from $5.37 billion in revenue in FY2023.
Systemwide, Ochsner reported 2024 operating revenue of $7.7 billion, operating income of $157.8 million (a 2.0% margin), net income of $243.1 million and 117 days cash on hand.
Ochsner's Schedule L for FY2024 reports conflict-of-interest transactions with interested persons; ProPublica's extract does not detail them.
Full-year 2025 audited results and the FY2025 Form 990 were not publicly extracted as of November 2026.
lobbying: Ochsner and its outside firms reported about $1.70 million in federal lobbying for 2025 in Senate LDA filings: $800,000 in-house plus Venable, The Picard Group and Mehlman Consulting ($200,000 each), Jones Walker ($170,000), Miller Strategies ($90,000) and Strategic Health Care ($37,500).

Through the first three quarters of 2026, Ochsner's federal lobbying totaled about $1.25 million, including $600,000 in-house and $450,000 paid to Miller Strategies, with Strategic Health Care, Cornerstone Government Affairs and Jones Walker also retained.
The jump in Miller Strategies billings, from $90,000 in 2025 to $450,000 in the first three quarters of 2026, makes it Ochsner's largest outside lobbying firm in 2026.
Ochsner maintains registered lobbyists with the Louisiana Board of Ethics; state spending totals were not verified for this dossier.
As an AHA trustee, November now helps steer the industry's main federal lobbying operation, which reported more than $25 million in in-house federal lobbying expenses in 2025.
revolvingDoor: No federal or state government employment is publicly reported for November; his career has been inside Ochsner's finance, legal-administrative and digital units.
Civic seats on the Business Council of New Orleans and the Committee of 100 place him inside Louisiana's main business-policy networks.
homeSystemRecord: Ochsner Health's charity care at cost was $82.4M (latest hospital tax returns).
Ochsner Health has 421 340B contract pharmacy arrangements registered with HRSA (OPAIS registry, Sept. 29, 2026).
Ochsner operates 47 hospitals and more than 370 health and urgent care centers across Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama, with about 40,000 employees as of 2025.

In May 2023, months into his tenure, November announced 770 layoffs (about 2% of staff) in management, administrative and clerical roles after Ochsner lost $96 million in 2022, its first unprofitable year in over a decade.
Ochsner's operating income recovered from a 2022 loss to $157.8 million in 2024, while November's pay rose 56% over FY2022-FY2024.

In December 2025 Ochsner signed a letter of intent for a non-merger clinical affiliation with Allegiance Health System, which runs rural hospitals in Louisiana, Texas and Mississippi; this extends Ochsner's referral reach without an acquisition review.
Ochsner's 2021 absorption of Rush Health System in Mississippi and Alabama and its earlier Lafayette General merger built it into the dominant system in much of Louisiana.
In March 2026 Ochsner began a collaboration with Cognito Therapeutics on an investigational neuromodulation device for Alzheimer's patients.
litigation: On March 24, 2026, a federal judge in the Eastern District of Louisiana dismissed for the second and final time a worker class action over Ochsner's use of forfeited 401(k) contributions, finding the amended complaint misstated the plan language.
No new False Claims Act settlements, antitrust suits or state attorney general actions against Ochsner in 2025 or 2026 were found in public reporting.
redFlags: November's pay jumped 46% in one year to $6.11 million plus $899,128 in other compensation in FY2024, while the system's operating margin was 2.0%.
A tax-exempt system with $325 million in FY2024 net income at its main entity pays at least two executives more than $6 million each.
His first major act as CEO in 2023 was cutting 770 jobs; executive pay then rose sharply as margins recovered.
Ochsner spent about $1.7 million on federal lobbying in 2025 and $1.25 million in the first nine months of 2026, with outside firm spending shifting heavily to Miller Strategies.
Ochsner's market dominance in Louisiana keeps growing through mergers and affiliation agreements, such as the 2025 Allegiance LOI, that avoid full merger review.
patternSummary: Pete November is a CPA and lawyer who rose through Ochsner's finance office and now runs Louisiana's dominant tax-exempt system. Under him Ochsner went from a 2022 loss to a $243 million net gain in 2024, helped by 770 layoffs, while his own pay climbed to more than $7 million in total compensation. Ochsner keeps a steady seven-figure federal lobbying operation and widens its regional footprint through affiliations rather than reviewable mergers. His AHA seat gives a high-paid Gulf Coast nonprofit executive a vote on the industry's federal lobbying agenda.

name: Philip O. Ozuah, MD, PhD
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Montefiore Medicine, the parent of Montefiore Health System and Albert Einstein College of Medicine, branded Montefiore Einstein; CEO since 2019 after serving as system president and, before that, EVP and COO.
Former Professor and University Chairman of Pediatrics at Einstein and Physician-in-Chief of the Children's Hospital at Montefiore.

AHA Board of Trustees: elected in August 2024 to fill a one-year unexpired term starting Jan. 1, 2025, per the AHA press release; he remains on the AHA's published board roster under President and CEO Steve Walsh.
Director of The Cigna Group since May 2023, a seat on the board of one of the largest commercial insurers that negotiates rates with hospitals like his own.
Director of Organon & Co. since 2021, where he chairs the Portfolio Development Committee and sits on the Talent Committee.
Board member of the New York City Police Foundation and the Federal Law Enforcement Foundation, per his Organon biography.
MD from the University of Ibadan, Nigeria; master's in education from USC; PhD in educational leadership from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln.
financial: Montefiore Medical Center's FY2024 Form 990 (EIN 13-1740114, filed Nov. 14, 2025) reports $5.91 billion in revenue, $5.62 billion in expenses and $288.6 million in net income for that entity.

Schedule J breakdown (FY2024, Montefiore Health System and four related returns): base salary $5.35M, bonus and incentive $7.09M, other reportable $4.20M, retirement and deferred $17,000, nontaxable benefits $33,767; total $16.69M. Bonus and incentive pay was 42% of the total.
The same filing reports Ozuah's FY2024 total compensation at $16.69 million: $0 from the hospital itself, $16.64 million from related organizations and $50,767 in other compensation.
His reported total rose from $9.91 million in FY2022 to $16.36 million in FY2023 and $16.69 million in FY2024, a 68% increase in two years.

Montefiore Health System posted an operating loss of $120.9 million (-1.4% margin) on $8.8 billion in operating revenue in 2025, versus $164.7 million in operating income in 2024; the 2025 net loss was $56.3 million.

The 2024 surplus rested on one-time government money: FEMA reimbursement fell from $254.9 million in 2024 to $1.2 million in 2025, and Montefiore said that without federal and state funds its 2024 margin would have been -2.4%.
In Q1 2026 the system lost $104.9 million from operations (-4.5% margin) amid the nurses' strike, and through June 30, 2026 it had lost $69.1 million (-1.5% margin) on $4.7 billion in revenue.

KBRA revised Montefiore Medical Center's outlook downward in 2026, citing debt service coverage falling to 1.29x from 3.4x and days cash on hand falling to 58 from 80; management targets structural balance only in 2027.
lobbying: Montefiore Medical Center lobbies Congress through Welsh Rose LLC, reporting $110,000 in each quarterly LDA filing from 2025 through Q3 2026, roughly $440,000 a year and $330,000 for the first three quarters of 2026.

Its 2025-2026 filings list the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's implementation, Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement, site-neutral payment, hospital price transparency, the 340B program, NIH funding, earmarks and, from Q4 2025, FEMA reimbursement.
CFO Colleen Blye publicly implored elected officials in May 2025 to keep 'partnering' with Montefiore on funding, noting about 85% of its patients have government coverage.
In 2026 Montefiore said it was working with New York State leaders to keep Managed Care Organization tax revenue flowing to hospitals.
As an AHA trustee, Ozuah helps govern the trade group that leads opposition to site-neutral payment and defends the 340B program, the same issues his own system lobbies on.
No personal federal political contributions by Ozuah were identified in this review.
revolvingDoor: Sits simultaneously on the board of The Cigna Group, a payer, and the AHA board, the provider lobby that fights payers over reimbursement and prior authorization.
Holds a pharmaceutical board seat at Organon while his health system lobbies on the 340B drug discount program, which pits hospitals against drugmakers.
Montefiore has repeatedly hired former Bronx elected officials, a pattern City & State New York reported on in 2024.
homeSystemRecord: Montefiore's charity care at cost was $99.0M (latest hospital tax returns).
Montefiore has 379 340B contract pharmacy arrangements registered with HRSA (OPAIS registry, Sept. 29, 2026).

About 15,000 NYSNA nurses at Montefiore, Mount Sinai and NewYork-Presbyterian struck beginning Jan. 12, 2026, the largest and longest nurses' strike in New York City history; Gov. Hochul declared a state of emergency.

Montefiore settled on Feb. 9, 2026 with a contract adding $15,000 to base wages over three years and running through December 2028; the three systems spent about $100 million on replacement nurses during the strike, per the Greater New York Hospital Association.
Striking nurses accused management of 'Bronx disinvestment' and corporate greed, contrasting Bronx emergency-department crowding with suburban investment.
In May 2026 Montefiore notified 12 utilization review nurses that their jobs would end July 12, 2026, as it automated the work with AI software; NYSNA filed a class grievance on June 1.

The Lown Institute's 2022 analysis of 2019 data found Montefiore Medical Center had a $76 million Fair Share surplus, the largest among 21 New York City hospitals studied, meaning its community spending exceeded its estimated tax-break value.
Montefiore is a 340B participant and lists the program among its federal lobbying issues; no public accounting of how 340B savings reach patients was found.
litigation: On Jan. 28, 2026, House Ways and Means Chairman Jason Smith and Rep. David Schweikert sent letters to Montefiore Medical Center and UChicago Medicine over New York Times reporting that the hospitals transplanted organs from American donors into wealthy foreign patients, demanding documents by Feb. 10, 2026 under threat of subpoena.
Smith said hospitals that prioritized foreign nationals over Americans 'should have their tax-exempt status terminated'; no public resolution of the inquiry has been reported as of November 2026.
redFlags: Ozuah's reported pay rose to $16.69 million in FY2024 while the system he runs swung to a $120.9 million operating loss in 2025 and asked lawmakers for more public money.
All of his compensation is reported through related organizations, with $0 shown at the hospital entity, which makes his pay harder for the public to trace on any single filing.
The 2018 'early retirement' payout of roughly $9 million, reported by the New York Post, went to an executive who did not retire but was promoted to CEO.
Montefiore is under a congressional inquiry into whether it gave American-donor organs to wealthy foreign patients, with the committee chairman openly raising revocation of tax-exempt status.
He serves as a director of Cigna while sitting on the AHA board, a direct conflict between payer fiduciary duty and provider-lobby governance.
Montefiore's 2024 'profit' depended on $254.9 million in FEMA money; stripped of public subsidies the system has not covered its costs since, and its credit outlook has been cut.
A record nurses' strike in 2026 followed by AI-driven nurse job cuts months later undercuts the system's public posture of investing in frontline care.
His AHA term status is opaque: AHA announced a one-year term for 2025 and has announced no re-election, yet he remains on the published roster.
patternSummary: Ozuah runs an $8.8 billion Bronx safety-net system that lives on government payers, federal disaster money and state tax transfers, and he is paid $16.7 million to do it. As the subsidies ebbed in 2025 the system swung to a $120.9 million operating loss, cut its credit outlook, endured a record strike and began automating nurse jobs, while his pay kept climbing. He sits on the boards of an insurer (Cigna), a drugmaker (Organon) and the hospital lobby (AHA) at once, and his flagship hospital faces a congressional inquiry that put its tax exemption in question.

name: Brian Peters
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of the Michigan Health & Hospital Association in Okemos, Mich., which represents Michigan's community hospitals. He has spent his whole career at MHA, rising through advocacy roles to CEO.
Also leads the MHA Health Foundation, a 501(c)(3), and the MHA Service Corporation, a fee-based services arm.
AHA Board of Trustees: elected August 2024 to a three-year term that began Jan. 1, 2025; he is listed on the current AHA roster.
Member of the AHAPAC Board of Directors, which steers the AHA's federal PAC.
Past chair of the AHA State Issues Forum and former member of AHA Regional Policy Board 5 and the AHA Committee on Nominations.
Director of Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan, the state's dominant insurer; BCBSM members re-elected him to its board on May 21, 2026, in the board's provider category.
financial: MHA's FY2025 Form 990 (year ending June 2025, EIN 38-1458751) reports Peters' compensation at $1,349,100 plus $159,670 in other compensation, about $1.51 million in total, up from about $1.32 million ($1,233,526 plus $89,489) in FY2024, a 14% raise.
MHA reported $61.95 million in revenue, $56.1 million in expenses and $5.8 million in net income in FY2025, and its net assets grew to $28.5 million from $22.7 million.
Almost half of MHA's FY2025 revenue ($30.4 million, 49.1%) was booked as contributions, mostly dues and grants from the hospitals it represents.
MHA's 990 discloses that it provided first-class or charter travel.
Two other MHA executives, both with the title Executive Vice President and Chief of Staff, were paid about $829,000 (Nancy McKeague) and $802,000 (Laura Appel) including other compensation in FY2025.
Corewell Health CEO Tina Freese Decker sat on MHA's own board (FY2024 990), linking the state association's governance to the system that held the AHA chair in 2025.
Any director fees Peters receives from BCBSM are a separate income stream disclosed in BCBSM's own filings, not MHA's 990.
lobbying: MHA spent $200,000 in 2025 and $150,000 in the first three quarters of 2026 on outside federal lobbyist Cornerstone Government Affairs ($50,000 a quarter), plus in-house federal lobbying by MHA staff (Senate LDA filings).

Its 2025 federal filings focus on Medicaid state directed payments, provider taxes and H.R. 1 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), plus Medicare site-neutral payment, telehealth waivers and the 340B program.

In 2026 MHA's lobbyists began monitoring H.R. 9504, the Tax-exempt Hospital Transparency Act, along with the Prices on the Wall Act (H.R. 9390) and the Lower Costs, More Transparency Act of 2026 (H.R. 9393), bills that target hospital pricing and tax-exempt status.

MHA's Health PAC reports $386,215 in total contributions and $455,741 in total expenditures on TransparencyUSA (period not specified). Its largest recipient is the AHA's federal PAC, AHAPAC, at $90,389, followed by the Michigan Senate and House Democratic caucus funds ($48,875 and $46,000).
As an AHAPAC board member, Peters helps direct the national hospital industry's federal campaign giving, which his own state PAC also funds.
MHA vigorously defends Michigan's certificate-of-need law, which blocks competitors from entering hospital markets.
revolvingDoor: Gov. Gretchen Whitmer appointed him to the Michigan Economic Recovery Council during COVID-19 and to the 2020 Census Complete Count Committee.
He sits on the board of BCBSM, the insurer that pays the hospitals he represents.
homeSystemRecord: Michigan now has three people on the AHA's published board roster: Peters, Trinity Health CEO Mike Slubowski (Livonia, term through 2028) and Corewell Health CEO Tina Freese Decker, whose past-chair term ends Dec. 31, 2026.
Corewell Health, MHA's largest member system, held the AHA chair in 2025 while Peters sat on the board.
In 2025 and 2026 Peters led MHA's campaign against federal Medicaid cuts in H.R. 1, warning publicly that the reductions would close Michigan hospitals.
MHA's 2026 federal agenda shifted toward 'affordability' and 340B defense, while its lobbyists tracked bills that would force hospital price posting and scrutinize tax exemption.
litigation: No 2025 or 2026 lawsuits or enforcement actions naming MHA or Peters surfaced in news and legal-database searches.

Michigan's hospital sector has a history of antitrust enforcement: the Justice Department and Michigan's attorney general sued four hospital systems, including Henry Ford Allegiance Health, over agreements not to compete for patients in marketing.
redFlags: He sits on both sides of the rate table: CEO of the Michigan hospital lobby and, re-elected in May 2026, a director of BCBSM, the state's dominant insurer.
His pay rose 14% to about $1.51 million in FY2025 at a trade association funded largely by dues from tax-exempt hospitals, and MHA's 990 discloses first-class or charter travel.
MHA's PAC routes its single largest contribution to AHAPAC, the national PAC whose board Peters sits on, so state hospital money flows into a federal fund he helps steer.
MHA is lobbying Congress against Medicaid cuts while also monitoring hospital price-transparency and tax-exemption bills, defending the revenue streams of systems that report healthy margins.
He defends certificate-of-need protection for incumbent hospitals in Lansing and brings that protectionism to the AHA board.

Michigan's outsized presence on the AHA board, with Corewell, Trinity and MHA all at the table and Corewell's CEO on MHA's own board, ties national hospital policy closely to Michigan's largest systems.
patternSummary: Peters is a career hospital lobbyist who has never worked outside the Michigan Health & Hospital Association and now helps govern the national lobby. He was paid about $1.51 million in FY2025, sits on the board of the state's dominant insurer while representing the hospitals that bill it, and runs a state PAC whose largest check goes to the AHA's own federal PAC. Together with Corewell and Trinity, he gives Michigan's hospital incumbents an unusually large voice at the AHA.

name: Richard J. Pollack
title: President & CEO Emeritus (former President & CEO)
affiliations: Served as AHA President & CEO from 2015 until his retirement in September 2026, when Steve Walsh, former CEO of the Massachusetts Health & Hospital Association, took over.

Spent 43 years at the AHA after joining in 1982, including more than 20 years as Executive Vice President for Advocacy and Public Policy, which made him the association's chief Washington lobbyist before he became CEO.
The AHA board voted in December 2025 to give him the title AHA President & CEO Emeritus, effective when the transition was complete; AHA was using that title for him by September 30, 2026.
Started his career as a legislative assistant to Rep. David Obey (D-Wis.), then worked as a legislative representative at the American Nurses Association starting in 1980 before moving to the AHA.
Received The Joint Commission's inaugural Lifetime Service Award, announced September 30, 2026. The Joint Commission is the accreditor whose seal hospitals rely on for Medicare deemed status.
Holds a bachelor's degree from SUNY Cortland and an MPA from American University.
financial: FY2024 Form 990: Pollack received $5,823,759 in reportable compensation plus $55,174 in other compensation, about $5.88 million in total. That is up roughly 71% from $3,396,123 in 2023.

Paddock Post's analysis of AHA 990s puts his pay at $2.50M (2017), $2.75M (2018), $4.70M (2019), $3.15M (2020), $3.14M (2021), $3.18M (2022) and $3.40M (2023), or about $23 million over 2017-2023. Adding FY2024 brings the eight-year total to about $29 million.
AHA FY2024 (calendar 2024) Form 990: revenue of $146.7 million against expenses of $169.3 million, a deficit of about $22.6 million. Net assets fell from $289.8 million to $277.6 million.
In 2023, AHA paid $78 million in compensation to 431 employees, an average of about $181,000. Its 16 highest-paid employees received about $17 million combined.

Other top FY2024 AHA pay: COO Michelle Hood got $1.92M, EVP Government Relations Stacey Hughes $1.70M plus $294K other, General Counsel Chad Golder $1.07M, SVP Chris DeRienzo $887K, and GVP Lisa Kidder Hrobsky $712K.
In a June 2026 statement, AHA credited Pollack with growing the association's net assets 57% through 2024, non-dues revenue 26% and total revenue 15%. Operating expenses also rose.
lobbying: AHA's Senate lobbying filings show $25.47 million in federal lobbying in 2025, Pollack's last full year as CEO, and roughly $194 million since 2018.
AHA reported about $10.55 million in federal lobbying for January-June 2026, down 20% from the first half of 2025, during the CEO transition year.
AHA spent $7 million on lobbying in Q1 2025 alone, working on Medicare financing, the healthcare workforce and the Medicaid provisions of the 2025 reconciliation bill.
The AHA PAC reported $1.81 million in receipts and $3.74 million in spending for the 2024 cycle, including $1.83 million in independent expenditures.
In his last months as CEO, Pollack led the fight against HHS's 340B rebate model. On July 31, 2026, he said AHA was 'considering all available options' to stop it, and AHA sued on October 9, 2026.
Pollack has described AHA's influence operation in terms of grassroots networks in every congressional district, PAC money, coalitions and advertising, calling grassroots 'absolutely king.'
revolvingDoor: His career ran from congressional staff (Rep. David Obey) to nurse-association lobbyist to AHA lobbyist to AHA CEO, a Washington insider path spanning more than 45 years.
As AHA's top lobbyist for more than two decades before becoming CEO, he was a registered federal lobbyist for the association.

His successor, Steve Walsh, also comes from government: six terms in the Massachusetts House, where he chaired the health care financing committee, followed by state hospital association CEO since 2017. The AHA board picked another lobbyist-legislator, not an operator.
As President & CEO Emeritus, Pollack keeps a formal title and public profile at the AHA after his retirement.
homeSystemRecord: AHA filed suit against HHS's hospital price transparency rule and lost in district court and again at the D.C. Circuit on December 29, 2020, clearing the rule to take effect January 1, 2021.

On December 1, 2025, AHA, the Maine Hospital Association and four health systems sued in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine to block HHS's 340B rebate pilot. Judge Lance Walker issued a preliminary injunction on December 29, 2025, the First Circuit denied a stay in January 2026, and HHS said on February 5, 2026 that it would scrap the pilot as designed.

After HHS revised and expanded the 340B rebate model for a January 1, 2027 start, AHA filed a second suit in the District of Maine on October 9, 2026, and on October 21, 2026 opposed drug-industry intervention in the case.

When the Senate HELP Committee majority staff found in October 2023 that 12 of 16 large nonprofit systems spent less than 2% of revenue on charity care, Pollack called the analysis 'just plain wrong.' He pointed to an AHA-commissioned EY study claiming about $9 in community benefit per $1 of tax exemption.
AHA has long opposed lifting the federal restrictions on physician-owned hospitals, a position that protects incumbent systems from physician-led competition.
litigation: American Hospital Association v. Azar (price transparency): AHA lost at the district court, and the D.C. Circuit affirmed on December 29, 2020.

AHA et al. v. HHS (340B rebate pilot, D. Maine, filed December 1, 2025): the preliminary injunction granted December 29, 2025 was upheld when the First Circuit denied a stay in January 2026, and HHS withdrew the pilot as designed in February 2026.

AHA et al. v. HHS (revised 340B rebate model, D. Maine, filed October 9, 2026): the suit seeks declaratory and injunctive relief to block the program before its January 1, 2027 start and was pending as of November 2026.
On October 2, 2026, AHA filed an amicus brief backing a hospital's challenge to an Eli Lilly 340B policy.
redFlags: His pay jumped to about $5.88 million in FY2024, up roughly 71% in one year, while the AHA ran a $22.6 million deficit and member hospitals were telling Congress they could not absorb Medicaid and site-neutral cuts.
Over 2017-2024 he collected about $29 million from a trade group funded mostly by dues from tax-exempt hospitals, so taxpayer-subsidized revenue ultimately paid for the lobbying chief.

Under him, AHA reported $25.47 million in federal lobbying in 2025, much of it spent to stop Medicaid financing reforms and site-neutral payment that would cut what Medicare pays for the same service depending on who owns the building.
He spent AHA money in court against price transparency (lost in 2020) and against 340B rebates (2025 and 2026), consistently opposing patients and payers seeing prices or auditing discounts.
He dismissed independent charity-care findings ('just plain wrong') and relied on an industry-commissioned EY study that counts Medicaid shortfalls and other self-reported items as community benefit.
He leaves with an emeritus title and a Joint Commission lifetime award, which keeps an industry lobbyist inside quality-oversight circles after retirement.
The board replaced him with another politician-lobbyist (Walsh), signaling that AHA treats its job as political defense of hospital revenue rather than reform.
patternSummary: Rick Pollack spent 43 years turning the AHA into one of Washington's most effective incumbent-protection machines, and left in September 2026 at the top of his earning power, with about $5.88 million in FY2024 pay and $25.47 million in federal lobbying in 2025. His tenure follows a consistent playbook: sue to block price transparency and 340B accountability, dismiss independent charity-care critiques, and fight any payment reform that pays equally for equal services. The board's choice of another career politician to replace him signals the strategy will not change.

name: Lisa Shannon
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Allina Health since January 1, 2022, after serving as Allina's president and COO under Penny Wheeler; Allina runs 12 hospitals in Minnesota and western Wisconsin.
If the Sutter Health combination closes, she is slated to stay on as president and CEO of Allina, which would become Sutter's Upper Midwest Division reporting up to Sutter CEO Warner Thomas.
AHA Board of Trustees: elected August 2024 to a three-year term that began January 1, 2025, and listed on the 2026 AHA roster; she has served on the AHA Health Systems Committee since 2023.
Prior executive roles at OhioHealth, Spectrum Health (now Corewell Health), where she was COO, and KentuckyOne Health (Catholic Health Initiatives).
financial: Allina reported a 2025 operating loss of $95.4 million (-1.6% margin) on $6.0 billion of operating revenue, worse than its $16.6 million operating loss in 2024; net income was $126.1 million thanks to investment returns.

Before restructuring charges, Allina lost $87 million on operations in 2025, compared with operating income of $48.6 million in 2024, and blamed payer recoupments, higher uncompensated care and rising supply costs.

Allina's 2024 results were flattered by a one-time gain from selling most of its outpatient lab business to Quest Diagnostics for about $230 million; it still posted a $16.6 million operating loss after restructuring costs.
Allina lost $321.4 million on operations (before restructuring) in 2023, so the system has been in or near the red for three straight years.
Allina Health System's FY2024 Form 990 shows about $5.9 billion in revenue, $5.8 billion in expenses and net income of about $94 million.

An earlier Form 990-based figure put Shannon's total compensation at about $3.08 million; at a July 2026 AG forum, a union speaker said her pay rose from $1.2 million in 2020 to over $4 million in 2024, a figure this review could not confirm against the filing.
A Sutter-Allina combination would create a roughly $26 billion, 39-hospital system; Sutter itself earned $509 million on operations (2.6% margin) in 2025 on $19.8 billion of revenue.
lobbying: Allina's federal lobbying totaled $190,000 in 2024 and $160,000 in 2025, all through Prime Policy Group, on health care and Medicare/Medicaid issues (Senate LDA filings).

In 2026 Allina dropped Prime Policy Group and hired Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath; combined 2026 spending through the third quarter was $110,000 ($20,000 on Prime's final report plus $90,000 through Faegre). The new filings add budget, homeland security and disaster issues.
The AHA itself reported $25.47 million in in-house federal lobbying in 2025 and $14.39 million in the first three quarters of 2026 (Senate LDA filings), the agenda trustees help set.
Allina is a dues-paying member of the AHA and the Minnesota Hospital Association, and leans on those trade groups for most of its policy work.
Minnesota has no certificate-of-need regime for hospital expansion; the main state check on Allina is the attorney general, whose merger-review powers the Legislature expanded in 2023.
revolvingDoor: No government appointments or regulatory roles for Shannon were identified in this review.
Her influence runs through business and trade groups: the AHA board, the Minnesota Business Partnership and the Itasca Project.
homeSystemRecord: Sutter Health and Allina signed a letter of intent on March 17, 2026, and a definitive agreement on May 21, 2026; Sutter pledged more than $2 billion of investment in Minnesota and western Wisconsin, and the parties target a close by the end of 2026.

Minnesota AG Keith Ellison opened a public review under the state's Health Care Transaction Law, sought comment in April 2026 and held forums in July 2026; as of late August 2026 no decision had been announced.

About 600 Allina primary and urgent care physicians, PAs and NPs (Doctors Council SEIU) held a one-day strike in November 2025 and ratified their first contract, a three-year deal, in April 2026 with more than 90% support.

About 150 Doctors Council SEIU physicians at Mercy Hospital's Coon Rapids and Unity (Fridley) campuses held a four-day strike starting September 14, 2026, after three years without a first contract, then reached a tentative three-year deal about a week later.
More than 60 Allina hospice nurses (SEIU Healthcare MN & IA) struck for one day on July 6, 2026, and for seven days starting September 11, 2026, seeking a first contract.

Allina closed the Faribault birth center and ended evening and weekend emergency surgery there on December 1, 2025, and ended pediatric admissions at Faribault on May 7, 2026, consolidating care in Owatonna.
Allina eliminated inpatient pediatrics at Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids in June 2024, telling its unionized physicians that inpatient pediatrics was 'not a core service.'
After its 2024 lab sale to Quest, union physicians called the transition a 'disastrous, chaotic mess.'
litigation: Minnesota AG Ellison confirmed an investigation into Allina's debt collection and billing practices in August 2023, after Allina was reported to cancel appointments for patients with large unpaid balances; Allina dropped the policy, and this review found no public resolution of the probe.
The AG's review of the Sutter combination is the main live legal exposure: the office can sue to block a deal it finds against the public interest.

In Popovich v. Allina Health (2020), the Minnesota Supreme Court held that hospitals can be vicariously liable for negligence by independent-contractor ER physicians under an apparent-authority theory.
No new 2025 or 2026 False Claims Act, antitrust or patient-debt lawsuits against Allina were identified in the sources reviewed.
redFlags: She is selling a Minnesota nonprofit to a California system with a record of antitrust settlements, after three years of operating losses, and is set to keep her job running it.
The 'nonprofit' Allina lost money on operations in 2023, 2024 and 2025 even while selling off its lab business, which suggests a structural problem rather than a one-year blip.
Executive pay has risen steeply even as operations lost money; unions claim her pay more than tripled from 2020 to 2024.
Allina has now faced strikes or strike threats from primary care physicians, hospitalists and hospice nurses within a single year, all fighting for first contracts.
Service cuts (Faribault obstetrics and pediatrics, Mercy inpatient pediatrics) fall hardest on rural and family patients, while the system tells regulators the merger will bring investment.
Allina's practice of canceling care for indebted patients drew an AG investigation and was dropped only after national press coverage.
As an AHA trustee she helps set a federal agenda (site-neutral opposition, defense of the 340B program, tax-exemption protection) that her own consolidating system benefits from.
patternSummary: Shannon runs a $6 billion nonprofit that has lost money on operations for three straight years and is now handing itself to Sutter Health in a $26 billion cross-market merger, with her staying in charge. On her watch Allina has cut rural obstetric and pediatric services, sold off its lab business and fought first contracts with physicians and nurses, while executive pay climbed. Her AHA seat lets her shape the federal protections that make this kind of consolidation pay.

name: Michael A. Slubowski
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President & CEO of Trinity Health (Livonia, MI), named to succeed the prior CEO in a December 2018 announcement after serving as President & COO from 2017; Trinity is a Catholic system with 88 hospitals in 23 states, 134,000 employees and $26.8 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue.
Elected to the AHA Board of Trustees for a three-year term beginning January 1, 2026.
Named one of Modern Healthcare's 100 Most Influential People in Healthcare for 2025, his fourth consecutive year.

Former President & CEO of SCL Health in Denver (about 2010-2017); earlier executive roles at Trinity Health, Henry Ford Health System, Samaritan Health Services (Phoenix) and Providence Hospital (Southfield, MI).
Board member of Universal Technical Institute (NYSE: UTI), a publicly traded for-profit trade school.
Trinity's advocacy works through the Catholic Health Association, Catholic Charities USA, the US Conference of Catholic Bishops and the Partnership for Medicaid coalition.
financial: Slubowski's reported compensation was $7,298,977 for fiscal 2025 (year ended June 30, 2025: $7,249,746 reportable plus $49,231 other), per Trinity Health Corporation's Form 990.

Schedule J breakdown (FY2025, Trinity Health Corporation): base salary $2.85M, bonus and incentive $3.41M, other reportable $989,597, retirement and deferred $20,425, nontaxable benefits $28,806; total $7.30M. Bonus and incentive pay was 47% of the total.
His pay climbed from $4.40 million in fiscal 2022 to $5.34 million in fiscal 2023, $5.83 million in fiscal 2024 and $7.30 million in fiscal 2025, a 66% rise in three years.

Trinity reported fiscal 2026 operating revenue of $26.8 billion, operating income before other items of $427.8 million (1.6% margin), and $281.1 million (1.1%) after $103.9 million in restructuring costs and $42.7 million in impairments.
Trinity's fiscal 2026 excess of revenue over expenses was $2.3 billion (8.1% net margin), driven by a $728.4 million jump in investment earnings.
Trinity held $17.4 billion in unrestricted cash and investments (251 days cash on hand) and $23.0 billion in net assets at June 30, 2026.

Trinity's financial assistance (charity care at cost) fell 15% to $263.9 million in fiscal 2026 from $310.0 million in fiscal 2025, about 1% of revenue; total IRS-defined community benefit was $1.37 billion.
Trinity reports Medicaid pays $500 million a year less than its costs and says the 2025 reconciliation law's Medicaid changes could push that loss above $1 billion annually.
lobbying: Trinity Health reported $960,000 in in-house federal lobbying in 2025 plus $120,000 paid to McDermott+, about $1.08 million total; through Q3 2026 it reported $550,000 in-house, $60,000 to McDermott+ and $10,000 to Cozen O'Connor Public Strategies.
Its Q3 2026 filing lists opposition to 340B program cuts and rebate models, opposition to Eli Lilly's 340B claims-data reporting demands, the Secure 340B Act and the 340B Patients Act.
Trinity also lobbied on the Tax Exempt Hospital Transparency Act (H.R. 9504), against Medicare site-neutral payment cuts, and against Medicaid cuts in H.R. 1.
Senate LDA records show about $928,000 in 2024 federal lobbying under the Trinity Health client name.
Slubowski publicly campaigned against the House-passed One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid provisions in 2025, citing CBO estimates of 7.6 million people losing coverage.
The AHA, where he is a trustee, reported $25.47 million in federal lobbying in 2025 and $14.39 million through Q3 2026.
