The bonus was paid while UMC had only 44.8 days cash on hand, a liquidity position its own board called in the red.
County counsel told commissioners they were contractually obligated to pay the bonus, showing a pay contract that guarantees executive upside regardless of the hospital's financial position.
Performance goals that drive his bonus were scored at 100% by a UMC board committee in the same year the hospital braced for $45.4 million in federal-policy losses.

About 37% of UMC's net revenue comes from supplemental government payments, so its CEO has a direct personal and institutional stake in the federal payment policy the AHA board sets lobbying priorities on.
A taxpayer-backed public hospital expanding Quick Care and primary care clinics into commercially insured markets competes against private providers with a government balance sheet behind it.
His safety-net credentials give AHA cover when it defends tax exemptions and 340B money that flow overwhelmingly to large private nonprofit systems that provide far less uncompensated care.

UMC's newest lab project rides on $44 million of public money, $35 million in federal pandemic relief routed through the state plus $9 million from the city, extending a government-funded hospital's footprint.
patternSummary: Van Houweling is a for-profit-trained operator who stabilized Las Vegas's county hospital and now draws more than $1 million a year as a public employee, with commissioners obligated by contract to pay his bonus even during job cuts and thin cash. UMC lives on Medicaid and supplemental government payments, so his AHA seat ties federal subsidy policy directly to his own hospital's survival and his own incentive pay. His public-hospital profile is useful cover for an association whose policy wins mostly benefit far wealthier private systems.

name: Robert Vissers, MD
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Boulder Community Health (BCH) since July 2015, after joining in 2014 as COO; BCH is an independent, community-owned nonprofit anchored by Foothills Hospital in Boulder.
AHA Board of Trustees: elected August 2024 to a three-year term that began January 1, 2025, and listed on the 2026 AHA roster; he is a Regional Policy Board 9 delegate.

Elected chairman of the Colorado Hospital Association board in September 2021 for the following year; he is not among CHA's current officers (Chair Margo Karsten of Banner Health, Chair-Elect Chris Thomas, Immediate Past Chair Jandel Allen-Davis, MD).
Board-certified emergency physician; earlier ran Northwest Acute Care Specialists, an emergency physician group that contracted with Legacy Health in Portland, and held Legacy leadership roles.
financial: BCH reported $488.7 million in revenue and $474.0 million in expenses on its FY2024 Form 990, for a surplus of about $14.7 million and total assets of about $857 million.
In FY2023, BCH reported $458.0 million in revenue, $449.2 million in expenses and a surplus of about $8.7 million, so revenue grew about 7% year over year.
Vissers is listed with compensation of $1,247,286 in BCH's most recent Form 990 data aggregated by CauseIQ (the fiscal year was not specified on the page).
As a 501(c)(3), BCH pays no income, property or sales tax on a campus in one of Colorado's most expensive counties.
lobbying: No federal lobbying registrations for Boulder Community Health were found in Senate LDA filings for 2024, 2025 or 2026; BCH relies on trade associations for advocacy.
The AHA itself reported $25.47 million in in-house federal lobbying in 2025 and $14.39 million in the first three quarters of 2026 (Senate LDA filings), the agenda trustees help set.
As CHA chair in 2021-2022, Vissers led Colorado's hospital lobby at the state capitol, including the period when Colorado enacted hospital price-transparency enforcement and debt-collection limits.
revolvingDoor: No government appointments for Vissers were identified.
His influence runs through industry bodies: AHA trustee and RPB 9 delegate, former CHA chair, and a reported leadership role in Vizient's independent-hospital network.
homeSystemRecord: The Boulder Valley Care Network, BCH's clinically integrated provider network, dissolved effective December 31, 2025, and terminated its fee-for-service and value-based payer contracts; BCH and the Boulder Valley IPA said they would move versions of those contracts to their own providers.
Foothills Hospital joined Kaiser Permanente's network for most of Boulder County's roughly 38,000 Kaiser members starting March 1, 2024 (excluding KP Select plans).
A February 2026 Colorado Hospital Association map of service closures lists three BCH closures: home health (June 2020), an urgent care (May 2022) and pediatric outpatient rehab (December 2022).

BCH remains independent; Vissers has said that options outside independence 'move us further away from our vision,' but the system relies on outside vendors, reportedly including Optum (UnitedHealth Group) for revenue-cycle work.
No 2025 or 2026 strikes, credit-rating actions, mergers or layoffs at BCH were identified in the sources reviewed.
litigation: No lawsuits, settlements, False Claims Act matters, antitrust actions or patient-debt suits involving BCH in 2025 or 2026 were identified in the sources reviewed.
BCH's compliance with Colorado's hospital price-transparency law could not be confirmed; the state's November 2025 evaluation report does not name BCH in its narrative text.
redFlags: BCH collects nonprofit tax exemptions on a high-value campus in affluent Boulder County, yet its charity care and community benefit figures remain unpublished in the sources reviewed.
Vissers' pay of about $1.25 million is high for a single-campus community hospital with a surplus margin of about 3%.
The collapse of the Boulder Valley Care Network at the end of 2025, including termination of value-based payer contracts, undercuts BCH's pitch as a high-quality, coordinated independent alternative.
He chaired the Colorado hospital lobby and now sits on the AHA board, so the 'independent community hospital' voice on the board is in fact a career trade-association insider.
BCH has trimmed services (home health, urgent care, pediatric outpatient rehab) while keeping its tax-exempt status and posting surpluses.
patternSummary: Vissers runs a roughly $490 million independent nonprofit hospital in one of Colorado's wealthiest counties and gives the AHA board its token 'independent community hospital' seat. He is a former chair of the Colorado hospital lobby, earns about $1.25 million, and leads a system whose charity care remains opaque and whose physician network dissolved at the end of 2025.

name: Steve Walsh
title: President & CEO
affiliations: The AHA board unanimously named him President & CEO on June 30, 2026, after a national search run by WittKieffer. He took over from the retiring Rick Pollack in September 2026, and the AHA executive team page now lists him as President and CEO.

He was President & CEO of the Massachusetts Health & Hospital Association (MHA), the trade group for more than 70 Massachusetts hospitals and health systems, from November 2017 until he moved to AHA in 2026.
From 2014 to 2017 he was executive director of the Massachusetts Council of Community Hospitals (MCCH), a hospital trade group. He resigned from the Legislature in January 2014 to take that job.
He was a Democratic state representative for the 11th Essex District (Lynn) from 2005 to January 2014, six terms in all. In 2011 he became House chair of the Joint Committee on Health Care Financing.

As the House's lead negotiator he wrote and steered Chapter 224 of 2012, the cost-containment law that created the Massachusetts Health Policy Commission (HPC) and the statewide cost-growth benchmark.
On July 25, 2025, Gov. Maura Healey appointed him to the HPC board, the agency he helped create, while he was still the state's top hospital lobbyist.
He is a member of ACHE and holds degrees from Wesleyan University, New England School of Law and the Harvard Kennedy School.
financial: MHA's FY2025 Form 990 (fiscal year ending September 2025) reports his compensation as $1,230,212 reportable plus $387,810 other, about $1.62 million in total.
His total MHA pay roughly doubled over five years: about $848,000 in FY2020, $979,000 in FY2021, $1.10 million in FY2022, $1.13 million in FY2023, $1.32 million in FY2024 and $1.62 million in FY2025.
MHA's FY2025 revenue was $13.2 million against $13.3 million in expenses. In FY2025 his pay equaled about 12% of the association's total revenue.
His FY2025 pay was about 60% more than his predecessor Lynn Nicholas received in FY2017 (about $1.0 million in total).
His AHA compensation is not yet public and will first show up on AHA's 2026 Form 990. For comparison, Pollack's 2024 AHA pay was about $5.88 million.
lobbying: Under Walsh, MHA was Beacon Hill's top-spending lobbying client in 2022 and 2023. In 2024 it ranked second, spending $1.1 million on lobbyists, just behind the Massachusetts Association of Health Plans at $1.3 million.

At the HPC's March 2023 benchmark hearing he said the cost-growth benchmark should be 'modernized' and its mechanics refreshed. A Lown Institute fellow first wrote that Walsh wanted the benchmark scrapped, then issued a clarification that he had called for re-imagining it.

At a March 2024 HPC hearing he called the statutorily required benchmark discussion 'a relic of the past.' Massachusetts health care cost growth was 8.6% from 2022 to 2023, more than double the 3.6% benchmark.

MHA's long-standing position on legislative price controls, set out in its comments on the 2017 Senate HEALTH Act, is that it 'is opposed to the imposition of artificial caps on rates.' MHA backed a price floor for low-paid hospitals in principle and opposed penalties aimed at the highest-priced 'top 3' hospitals.

In 2024 MHA lobbied to protect hospitals' 340B program revenue inside MassHealth. It backed a Senate budget amendment to 'prohibit further erosion of a critical component of hospital financing' and fought a MassHealth bulletin limiting reimbursement for some 340B-purchased drugs.

On federal out-of-network billing, he praised Rep. Richard Neal's December 2020 surprise billing deal, which became the No Surprises Act, as 'fair and balanced.' That deal used arbitration rather than a benchmark payment rate.
AHA, which he now runs, reported $25.47 million in federal lobbying in 2025, and $14.39 million in the first three quarters of 2026.
revolvingDoor: In January 2014 he resigned his House seat, while still a sitting legislator, to run a hospital trade group (MCCH). He had chaired the committee that wrote the hospital cost law.
He wrote the law that created the Health Policy Commission, then lobbied it for hospitals as MHA CEO, then was appointed to its board in July 2025 while still MHA CEO.
His HPC seat is the 'hospital expertise' seat created by the 2024 market oversight law. The same law eliminated the board seats for a primary care physician and a business purchaser.

The Employer Coalition on Health called his HPC appointment 'a blatant conflict of interest' because he was a registered lobbyist. The Greater Boston Interfaith Organization argued that state conflict-of-interest law barred him from serving.

His recusal pledge covered only material change notices, determination of need applications and performance improvement plans from MHA members. He said he would be 'internally walled off' from MHA matters going to the HPC.
Whether he has formally left the HPC board since joining AHA has not been publicly reported in the sources reviewed.
The AHA board replaced one career lobbyist-insider (Pollack) with another: legislator, then trade-group chief, then regulator-commissioner.
homeSystemRecord: MHA under Walsh represented the hospitals in the country's most heavily studied cost-control regime. The 3.6% benchmark was blown through, with 8.6% growth from 2022 to 2023, and Walsh's response was to call the benchmark process outdated.
MHA argued in 2024 that Massachusetts commercial payers paid 195.3% of Medicare for hospital services, ranked 46th nationally, and that commercial rates reflect government underpayment.

The 2024-2025 market oversight law ('An Act Enhancing the Market Review Process,' H.5159), passed after Steward Health Care's collapse, expanded HPC review to private equity, REIT and MSO deals. It bars licensing hospitals whose main campus is leased from a health care REIT and raises CHIA late-filing penalties from $1,000 to $25,000.

MHA's own coverage of the oversight law took no stated position on it. The sources reviewed do not show a public Walsh position on the Steward collapse beyond State House remarks listing it as a crisis.

As AHA CEO, his stated early priorities in an October 26, 2026 AHA interview were a listening tour (Georgia, Wyoming, Chicago, D.C., Ohio, then California and Texas), drafting a strategic plan after the tour, and giving hospitals 'the room and the resources and the voice' to lead.

In the same interview he called preserving hospitals' community benefit role his top job and said health care's next phase will be shaped 'by us or to us.' 2026 Chair Marc Boom flagged the 2025 reconciliation law's Medicaid cuts, the 340B program and site-neutral payment as near-term fights.
litigation: No personal litigation or enforcement action involving Walsh has been publicly reported.
The GBIO conflict-of-interest objection to his HPC appointment was raised in a letter to the governor. No State Ethics Commission ruling against him has been reported.
redFlags: He wrote the 2012 cost-containment law, lobbied the agency it created for the hospital industry, then took a seat on that agency's board while still the industry's chief lobbyist.
He left the Legislature mid-term in 2014 to take a hospital trade-group job, after chairing the committee that wrote hospital financing law.

With Massachusetts health care cost growth at 8.6% against a 3.6% benchmark, the hospital lobby's answer under Walsh was to call the benchmark discussion 'a relic of the past' rather than accept accountability.
MHA opposes 'artificial caps' on hospital rates in a state where hospital prices drive cost growth, and it fought to protect 340B program margins inside Medicaid.
His MHA pay rose about 91% in five years, to $1.62 million in FY2025, about 12% of the association's revenue.
The 2024 oversight law that gave him his HPC seat also stripped the board's business-purchaser and primary care seats, tilting the cost regulator toward providers.

AHA hired a politician-lobbyist rather than an operator, which signals that the association's job remains political defense of hospital revenue: site-neutral payment, the 340B program and tax exemption.
patternSummary: Steve Walsh is a career Massachusetts insider. He was a six-term legislator who wrote the state's hospital cost-control law, then ran two hospital trade groups, then sat on the commission his own law created while still the industry's top lobbyist. At MHA he defended hospitals against rate caps and benchmark enforcement as costs grew at more than twice the target, and his pay rose to $1.62 million. The AHA board picked him to bring that playbook to Washington.

name: Erik Wexler
title: President & CEO
affiliations: President and CEO of Providence since January 1, 2025, succeeding Rod Hochman, MD; previously Providence's president and COO and president of strategy and operations for its southern region.
Joined Providence in May 2016 as senior vice president and CEO of its Southern California region.
Before Providence, served as CEO of Tenet Healthcare's Northeast Region, overseeing hospitals in Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Illinois.
Joined the board of Truveta, the health-system-owned data company, in March 2026, replacing Hochman.
AHA trustee with a term running through 2028.
financial: Wexler's total 2024 compensation was $9,125,384 ($8,590,356 reportable plus $535,028 other), per the Form 990 of Providence Health & Services - Washington.

Schedule J breakdown (FY2024, Providence Health & Services - Washington and eight related returns): base salary $1.97M, bonus and incentive $6.17M, other reportable $448,548, retirement and deferred $519,036, nontaxable benefits $15,992; total $9.13M. Bonus and incentive pay was 68% of the total.
His reportable pay rose 67% in one year, from $5,154,374 in 2023 to $8,590,356 in 2024, and has more than quadrupled from $1,864,281 in 2020.
Providence reported 2025 operating revenue of $29 billion and an operating loss of $132 million, or $486 million after $354 million in restructuring costs, with a $238 million net loss.

For the first half of 2026, Providence reported $175 million in operating income on $15 billion in revenue, compared with a $225 million operating loss a year earlier on a restated basis that excludes discontinued operations.
Q2 2026 operating income was $64 million, a 0.8% margin, after Q1 2026 operating income of $111 million (1.5%).
Moody's downgraded Providence St. Joseph Health from A2 to A3 with a stable outlook on July 1, 2025, citing persistent operating challenges, labor costs and Oregon's new presumptive charity care law.
Wexler told employees at the start of 2026 that Providence would spend more than $600 million on raises, which he said was possible because of 2025's hard decisions.
lobbying: Providence St. Joseph Health reported $800,000 in federal lobbying for 2025 in Senate LDA filings: $560,000 in-house and $240,000 paid to Mehlman Consulting.
Through the first three quarters of 2026, Providence reported $690,000 in federal lobbying ($510,000 in-house, $180,000 to Mehlman Consulting), on pace to exceed 2025.

Providence blamed rising Medicaid costs, insurer claim denials, local taxes and expected cuts from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act for its 2026 layoffs, which match the main federal and state fights it lobbies on.
revolvingDoor: No government employment is publicly reported for Wexler; his career has been in nonprofit and investor-owned hospital management, moving from Tenet to Providence in 2016.
His Truveta board seat links him to a data venture owned by dozens of large health systems that sells de-identified patient data for research.
homeSystemRecord: Providence's charity care at cost was $248M (latest hospital tax returns).
Providence has 1,050 340B contract pharmacy arrangements registered with HRSA (OPAIS registry, Sept. 29, 2026).
Providence runs about 51 hospitals and roughly 1,000 clinics across seven states, with more than 120,000 employees.

Headcount fell by about 5,000 in 2025 through divestitures and several rounds of layoffs; further cuts of about 296 positions at Providence Swedish in Washington and more than 150 in Oregon were announced for early 2026.
Wexler's first weeks as CEO coincided with a 46-day strike by nurses across eight Oregon Nurses Association units, which ended in February 2025 with raises of up to 22% and new staffing rules.

Divestitures under Wexler include 10 skilled nursing facilities sold to Ensign Group (2025), home health and hospice moved into a Compassus joint venture (2025), and Tegria and MedPearl sold in January 2026.
Providence Health Plan, which lost $102 million on $2.5 billion in revenue in 2025, will shut down most of its insurance business in 2027.

Providence plans to sell Queen of the Valley Medical Center in Napa to NorthBay Health by the end of 2026 and to phase out acute care and emergency services at Mission Hospital Laguna Beach, citing about $300 million in seismic upgrade costs.

In February 2024 Providence agreed to provide $157.8 million in refunds and debt relief to 99,446 Washington patients to resolve the state attorney general's charity care suit, which alleged it billed and sent eligible low-income and Medicaid patients to collections.
litigation: In February 2026 Providence agreed to a proposed $42.7 million settlement of an ERISA class action alleging it mismanaged its 401(k) plan and shifted plan costs onto participants; Providence denies wrongdoing and the deal requires court approval.

The Washington attorney general's charity care case ended in a February 2024 consent resolution requiring $137.2 million in debt forgiveness, $20.6 million in refunds and more than $4.5 million to the AG's office; Providence did not admit wrongdoing.
Moody's cited Oregon's new presumptive charity care law as a pressure on Providence's margins, signaling continuing regulatory exposure on billing low-income patients.
redFlags: Wexler's reportable pay rose 67% to $8.59 million in 2024, the year before he took over as CEO, while Providence was losing hundreds of millions on operations.
Providence cut about 5,000 jobs in 2025, booked $354 million in restructuring costs and posted a $238 million net loss, yet the CEO-designate's pay climbed sharply.

Washington's attorney general found Providence trained staff to 'ask every patient every time' for payment and sent Medicaid enrollees to collections; the system paid $157.8 million in relief in 2024.
Providence is closing acute and emergency care at Mission Hospital Laguna Beach and exiting most of its health plan business, reducing services while keeping its tax exemption.
Moody's downgraded Providence to A3 in July 2025 on persistent operating weakness.
The proposed $42.7 million 401(k) settlement in 2026 adds employee benefits mismanagement claims to the system's record.
patternSummary: Erik Wexler, a former Tenet regional executive, took over Providence in 2025 after a 67% raise to $8.59 million. His turnaround has relied on about 5,000 job cuts, selling off nursing homes, home health and IT units, winding down the health plan and closing acute care at a coastal hospital, which returned the system to thin operating gains in 2026. Providence's record includes a $157.8 million Washington charity care settlement and a 2026 retirement plan settlement. On the AHA board he represents a large tax-exempt system that is cutting services and staff while paying executives at for-profit levels.
